conflicts.issue: Decommitting Trail Connections in Harmony Road II / Chamberlain Subdivision (Z1400008)
conflicts.summary: Council split 5-2 over whether to release Standard Pacific from a 2006 committed element to build an asphalt trail connecting Chamberlain to Woodcroft's trail system and a southern mulch trail.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve removing the trail commitments because Woodcroft refused an off-site easement and Chamberlain residents negotiated a $75,000 recreation fund compromise.
side_a_arguments: Woodcroft Community Association formally rejected four to six proposed alignments across its private property.
Chamberlain residents agreed to redirect the $75,000 trail budget (net of legal/consulting costs) toward neighborhood recreation amenities.
Existing zoning lacked a timing trigger, and off-site easements beyond a developer's property boundary should not be enforced.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose decommitting the trails in order to preserve critical off-road pedestrian/bicycle connectivity to Southwest Elementary School and the Third Fork Creek Trail.
side_b_arguments: BPAC and residents rely on off-road trail links rather than forcing children onto city streets.
Removing the developer's commitment pushes the eventual cost of completing the Third Fork Creek tributary trail onto city taxpayers.
Woodcroft itself benefited from visionary trails, and the developer should pursue another alignment (such as toward Brindhurst/Tall Oaks) or mediation.
conflicts.resolution: Approved 5-2 (Catotti and Schewel voting no), removing the trail commitments.

conflicts.issue: Repeal of the $1.80/Month Solid Waste Collection Fee vs. Property Tax Replacement (Item 10D & Final Budget)
conflicts.summary: Council divided 4-3 on repealing the $1.80/month solid waste collection fee and replacing its $1.4 million revenue with property taxes, leading Eugene Brown to vote no (6-1) on the final overall budget.
conflicts.side_a_position: Repeal the flat $1.80/month ($21.60/year) solid waste fee and fund the $1.4 million through the property tax rate.
side_a_arguments: A flat per-household fee is regressive, charging a $75,000 homeowner or low-income renter the same $21.60/year as a $500,000 homeowner.
Any homeowner below ~$370,000 in assessed value—and single-family/duplex renters who pay $0 directly under property tax—pays less under Option 1.
Keeping the fee would require a 56% fee hike next year to cover a projected $800,000 solid waste shortfall.
conflicts.side_b_position: Retain the $1.80/month solid waste user fee to stabilize the solid waste enterprise fund and avoid raising property taxes.
side_b_arguments: The $20 million solid waste fund already receives $9.6 million in general-fund property tax subsidies from all property owners, including businesses and multi-family residents without city pickup.
Like DATA bus fares, a modest $1.80/month user fee for households receiving collection service is not regressive, and DSS assistance covers hardship cases.
Replacing the fee plus county/other increases risks giving Durham the highest municipal property tax rate among North Carolina's largest cities, hurting competitiveness.
conflicts.resolution: Option 1 repeal passed 4-3; the remaining FY 2014-15 budget ordinances then passed 6-1 with Eugene Brown dissenting because the final budget incorporated the fee repeal.

conflicts.issue: Phillips Research Park Apartments Impact Fee Appeal – Strict Code Enforcement vs. Equitable Tolling for Neighbor Litigation Delays
conflicts.summary: Council split 6-1 in upholding staff's denial of Phillips Research Park Apartments' appeal of a $108,000 impact fee increase incurred after a competitor's zoning appeals froze the project from 2008 until building permits were filed under the higher 2009 fee schedule, with Eugene Brown dissenting and Eddie Davis exploring a compromise split.
conflicts.side_a_position: Uphold the Impact Fee Appeal Committee and staff determination applying the July 1, 2009 impact fee schedule in effect when the building permit application was submitted.
side_a_arguments: City Code strictly mandates that impact fees be calculated at the time a completed building permit application is submitted (here 2010-2011), leaving Council and the Impact Fee Appeal Committee no legal authority to retroactively apply expired 2008 rates.
While the neighboring competitor's appeals caused hardship, Planning staff followed mandatory UDO stay provisions and the application also sat with the developer for extended periods.
Granting retroactive fee relief to one developer could expose the city to legal challenges and refund demands from other developers affected by fee or regulatory changes.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defer the appeal back to the City Manager rather than upholding the higher 2009 fee assessment, citing inadequate Planning Department communication and notification to the developer.
side_b_arguments: Planning staff failed to communicate effectively with the developer regarding the impact fee change and could have communicated more forcefully regarding the neighboring owner's interconnection obligations.

Because the developer relied on 2007 staff reliance letters, closed a $23 million loan in 2008, and was stalled by third-party litigation outside its control, Council should send the matter back to the Manager for further review rather than deny relief.
conflicts.resolution: Councilmember Steve Schewel's motion to uphold the staff and Impact Fee Appeal Committee determination passed 6-1, with Councilmember Eugene Brown voting No (while Councilmember Eddie Davis noted he would have favored splitting the increase in half if legally permissible but did not offer a substitute motion after Schewel's motion carried).

conflicts.issue: Hope Valley Farms Pod BB Rezoning for Murphy USA Fuel Station & Convenience Store (Z13-0012)
conflicts.summary: Council split 5-2 on removing a 2009 prohibition on fuel sales and convenience stores at 1051 Martin Luther King Jr. Parkway after neighboring Elm Grove Townhouse residents requested a continuance and council members scrutinized building aesthetics.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the rezoning (with an added four-sided brick exterior commitment) without further delay.
side_a_arguments: City and applicant met all statutory notification rules, including first-class letters to 45 property owners and the Elm Grove Townhouse Association.
The site has been zoned Commercial General since 2009, lies 500 feet from the nearest townhomes behind a 0.8 opacity vegetative buffer, and adds $2 million in tax base.
Applicant amended design commitments on reconsideration to mandate a brick exterior on all four walls.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose approval or delay action in light of Elm Grove neighborhood concerns.
side_b_arguments: Questioned whether affected Elm Grove townhome residents had adequate opportunity to review the proposal given their HOA board transition.
Raised compatibility and neighborhood impact concerns for the convenience store and fuel station.
conflicts.resolution: Initially passed 5-2, reconsidered 7-0 to secure a four-sided brick exterior commitment, and re-approved 5-2.

conflicts.issue: Acquisition of East Main Street / Carpenter Motor Company Site for New Police Headquarters
conflicts.summary: Council divided 6-1 over acquiring 4.523 acres along East Main Street for ~$5.69 million (plus demolition) for a new police headquarters and 911 complex, with Eugene Brown dissenting on cost and appraisal grounds while other members supported the site while pressing for urban design, retail activation, and historic/transit trade-offs.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the GWC Properties and W.T. Wilkerson land acquisition options to secure a consolidated central East Main Street site for police and 911 operations.
side_a_arguments: Extensive site search ruled out Fayetteville Street (planned for DHA redevelopment) and showed rebuilding on the existing site was cost-prohibitive.
Police and 911 departments wholeheartedly endorse the site, and GWC tenant rents during 2015 help offset the purchase premium over appraisal.
Staff committed to public design forums to improve Main Street walkability, streetscape, and potential public-private retail partnerships.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose the acquisition due to excessive cost (~$1.33M/acre plus demolition), reliance on a single appraisal, and paying 2.5x appraised value for the Hood Street parcel.
side_b_arguments: The city normally obtains two appraisals for major real estate acquisitions, whereas only one appraisal was done per property here.
Combined acquisition and $300,000-$400,000 demolition costs total roughly $6 million, representing an exceedingly high price per acre.
Public speakers also objected to demolishing the historic 1928 and 1948 Carpenter Motor Company buildings and questioned spending $6 million on a large headquarters.
conflicts.resolution: Approved 6-1; General Services proceeded with geotechnical/environmental due diligence and committed to public design forums and periodic Council updates.

conflicts.issue: Austin Lawrence Partners (City Center / Jack Tar) Incentive Agreement – Minimum Guaranteed Property Tax Yield vs. Capital Investment Metric
conflicts.summary: Mayor Bill Bell dissented in a 6-1 vote on the $3.97 million, 15-year incentive agreement for the City Center tower and Jack Tar Motel redevelopment, insisting the contract include an absolute minimum annual property tax yield ($327,400) rather than relying solely on capital investment thresholds, while the six council members and city finance/legal staff supported approving the agreement as drafted under existing policy.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the $3.97M incentive agreement immediately as drafted under existing economic development policy, relying on conservative tax assessor estimates ($60.9M assessed value) and avoiding constitutional tax-rebate risks.
side_a_arguments: Existing city policy bases incentives on qualified capital investment ($65M minimum) rather than actual tax revenue yields because directly linking incentives to tax revenues or requiring make-up payments risks violating the North Carolina Constitution's prohibition on tax rebates.

Finance staff already applied conservative buffers by basing projections on the tax assessor's $60.9M valuation (about 10% below the $65M minimum investment), capping the incentive at ~80.9% of projected property tax, and excluding ~$3.4M in projected hotel occupancy and sales taxes.
Delaying approval past April would disrupt the developer's imminent REIT financing term sheet and push back demolition and construction timelines.
conflicts.side_b_position: Hold the agreement until Thursday and amend Section 2.1 (or attach Exhibit D) to guarantee that the project generates at least $327,400 annually in general fund property tax revenue regardless of future property revaluations.
side_b_arguments: While the city's 15-year payout (~$265K/year) is fixed in dollars, future countywide property revaluations typically lower tax rates and could erode actual property tax inflows below the $327,400 projection.

Future councils paying out general fund dollars over 15 years should have contractual certainty of the minimum property tax revenue returning to the general fund rather than relying on non-binding memos or uncertain sales/hotel taxes.
conflicts.resolution: Council rejected Mayor Bell's request to hold the item until Thursday and approved the incentive agreement 6-1, with Bell voting No; City Attorney Fred Lamar agreed to examine revenue-guarantee mechanisms during the upcoming comprehensive Economic Development Policy overhaul.

conflicts.issue: Article 6 UDO Density Revisions and Impact on Transit-Oriented Growth & Affordable Housing (TC1200012)
conflicts.summary: During the public hearing on Item 15, the Inter-Neighborhood Council opposed residential density increases unrelated to transit access, and Council Members Don Moffitt and Eddie Davis scrutinized whether raising baseline densities undermined affordable housing bonuses or warranted delaying residential provisions.
conflicts.side_a_position: Adopt the revised Article 6 density adjustments and corridor bonuses as proposed by Horvath Associates and Planning staff.
side_a_arguments: Rounding fractional densities (at most 0.5 units/acre) and extending roadway bonuses to service roads and commercial/office districts encourages mixed-use redevelopment along major corridors.
Any higher density in RSM/RUM districts still requires a development plan approved by City Council, and service-road bonuses require direct access.
Density bonuses in the UDO can stack cumulatively, and affordable housing requires broader tools beyond density alone (Steve Medlin).
conflicts.side_b_position: Delay or reject the residential density provisions until density is directed toward walkable, transit-served areas and affordable housing bonuses are protected.
side_b_arguments: Allowing extra residential density outside transit corridors risks car-dependent sprawl (Pat Carstensen / Inter-Neighborhood Council).
Increasing by-right or baseline unit counts could reduce developers' incentive to use the affordable housing density bonus (questioned by Don Moffitt).
conflicts.resolution: Following staff clarifications that development plans still come before Council and that Planning will pursue non-density affordable housing incentives, Council unanimously approved TC1200012 by a 7-0 vote.

conflicts.issue: Awarding WIA Youth Contract to Out-of-County Provider Over Durham Applicant (Item 4)
conflicts.summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden dissented against awarding a Workforce Investment Act youth contract to Raleigh-based Community Partnerships, Inc. over Durham-based Operation Breakthrough.
conflicts.side_a_position: Follow the Workforce Development Board's recommendation to award the contract to Community Partnerships, Inc.
side_a_arguments: CPI scored higher overall (89 vs. 88.5) and consistently met federal and state WIA performance goals.
Workforce board members cited a recent audit of Operation Breakthrough and concerns about continuity under Operation Breakthrough's six-month intern staffing model.
conflicts.side_b_position: Prioritize Durham-based contractors and invest in mentoring local organizations rather than awarding contracts outside the city.
side_b_arguments: A half-point scoring margin (89 vs. 88.5) should not outweigh keeping public workforce dollars with a local Durham provider.
City staff should proactively mentor local firms like Operation Breakthrough so they can compete effectively for city contracts.
conflicts.resolution: Contract awarded to Community Partnerships, Inc. by a 6-1 vote.

conflicts.issue: Hanover Point UDO Road Connection to McLamb Drive (Z1400004)
conflicts.summary: Residents along McLamb Drive, Bristolwood Drive, and Danbury Road opposed connecting Hanover Point (Willow Crest Road) to McLamb Drive due to narrow, deteriorating state-maintained roads, while Council approved the rezoning 6-0 because the connection was required by UDO connectivity rules and already dedicated in 2006.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the Z1400004 rezoning to reduce density from 68 to 41 single-family homes while maintaining the previously dedicated UDO street connection.
side_a_arguments: Denying the rezoning leaves the 2006 approval intact, allowing 68 higher-density homes while still requiring the exact same McLamb Drive connection.
UDO connectivity standards mandate tying into dedicated stub roads for emergency access and interconnected neighborhoods.
Most Hanover Point traffic will travel south through modern city-standard Ashton Hall streets rather than north onto deteriorating state roads.
conflicts.side_b_position: Oppose connecting Willow Crest Road to McLamb Drive and direct new development traffic elsewhere until roads are upgraded.
side_b_arguments: McLamb and Bristolwood are 18-foot-wide, uncurbed 1984 tar-and-gravel state roads already disintegrating into dirt.
Cut-through commuters heading north toward Highway 98 and Wake Forest will accelerate road deterioration without developer or NCDOT repair funding.
32 neighbors signed a petition favoring use of an alternate future connector stub further from existing homes.
conflicts.resolution: Approved 6-0; Council advised residents to petition NCDOT (including former Durham Mayor Nick Tennyson) or consider voluntary city annexation for street maintenance.

conflicts.issue: Montclair Phase II Boundary: 1,000-Foot Chain-Link Fence vs. 25-Foot Undisturbed Buffer (Item 7)
conflicts.summary: Adjacent property owner Michael Hining urged Council to reject Montclair Phase II unless the developer built a 1,000-foot chain-link fence separating the subdivision from his 12-acre farm, whereas the developer refused the fence and offered a 25-foot undisturbed buffer.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the rezoning with a 25-foot undisturbed buffer along the shared property line without requiring a chain-link fence.
side_a_arguments: A chain-link fence is ineffective because people can climb over or walk around it, and law enforcement already addresses trespassing.
Requiring fences along every property line with potential foot traffic would set an unworkable precedent across Durham.
A 25-foot undisturbed buffer adds 15 feet beyond the 10-foot code minimum and benefits both the neighbor and new homeowners (Jared Edens for David Weekley Homes).
conflicts.side_b_position: Deny the rezoning unless the developer installs a chain-link fence along the 1,000-foot boundary.
side_b_arguments: The neighboring 12-acre farm contains ponds and over 50 fruit trees that pose an attractive nuisance and child safety hazard.
Phase II doubles the nearby housing count and number of children, and a 25-foot buffer or no-trespassing signs will not stop children from entering the farm (Michael Hining).
conflicts.resolution: While Council Member Steve Schewel acknowledged struggling with the request, Council accepted the 25-foot undisturbed buffer proffer and approved Montclair Phase II 6-0.

conflicts.issue: Acceptance vs. Mere Receipt of the Durham Traffic Separation Study (TSS) Recommendations (Item 28)
conflicts.summary: Council tied 3-3 on adopting a resolution accepting the Durham Traffic Separation Study recommendations, then voted 6-0 merely to receive the report without endorsing its conceptual street closures.
conflicts.side_a_position: Approve the staff-recommended resolution accepting the TSS report with caveats requiring future project-specific studies and public input.
side_a_arguments: The resolution explicitly conditioned any implementation on subsequent project-specific studies, public engagement, and City Council approval.
Accepting the final report concluded the study phase while preserving Council veto power over individual rail crossings.
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject the approval resolution and merely receive the report so conceptual closures like Dillard Street are not treated as adopted city policy.
side_b_arguments: Accepting recommendations lacking broad community support creates an expectation that projects like closing Dillard Street are moving forward.
Durham Area Designers noted the limited scenarios evaluated were conceptual at best and potentially damaging to downtown livability.
conflicts.resolution: The resolution accepting the TSS recommendations failed on a 3-3 tie (Diane Catotti absent), and Steve Schewel's motion merely to receive the report passed 6-0.

conflicts.issue: FY 2014-2015 Budget Guidelines – Scope and Tax Level of Dedicated Parks Funding ('Penny for Parks')
conflicts.summary: Council debated whether dedicated property tax funding for parks should be used for new facilities and land expansion or restricted strictly to maintenance and renovation of existing assets, and weighed tax/fee burdens on lower-income residents before settling on an informational study capped at 1 cent solely for maintenance and renovation.
conflicts.side_a_position: Limit any dedicated parks funding strictly to maintaining and renovating existing parks and trails (no new facilities or land acquisition) and study up to 1 cent alongside peer-city tax/fee and park policing data.
side_a_arguments: Existing parks and recreation facilities face severe deferred maintenance deficiencies that must be addressed before building new facilities or buying land.
Raising taxes without clear maintenance priorities, police protection of park assets, and analysis of cumulative water/sewer/stormwater/solid-waste burdens could hurt low-income residents.
conflicts.side_b_position: Seek new parks facilities in addition to maintenance and renovation (initially championed by Steve Schewel before conceding a 6-1 council majority against new facilities, shifting to a 0.5-cent maintenance/renovation study).
side_b_arguments: A majority of Council still supported exploring dedicated funding for parks and trails maintenance and renovation so Council could review concrete service-level options between 0 and 0.5 cents (or up to 1 cent) during budget workshops.
Underutilized small parks could also be evaluated for repurposing rather than purely selling or abandoning.
conflicts.resolution: Councilmember Steve Schewel conceded on record that his push for new parks facilities lacked support (6-1) and moved an amended guideline—approved 7-0—directing staff to present a specific plan for parks and trails maintenance and renovation at funding levels not to exceed 1 cent per $100 assessed value.

conflicts.issue: Police Consent Search Policy, Marijuana Enforcement, and Community Trust (Item 4: City Manager's HRC/CPRB Report)
conflicts.summary: While Council did not vote on Item 4, council members pressed City Manager Tom Bonfield and DPD leadership to go further than the manager's report on mandatory written consent forms for vehicle searches and lowering enforcement priority for low-level marijuana offenses.
conflicts.side_a_position: Require written consent forms for all consensual vehicle searches, deprioritize low-level marijuana arrests, and expand neighborhood foot patrols and informant protections.
side_a_arguments: Young Black men report arbitrary stops, making written consent forms urgent and legally permissible.
High marijuana arrest rates among African American males induct young people into the criminal justice system despite polling favoring treatment.
McDougald Terrace residents want officers out of patrol cars walking neighborhoods and stronger confidentiality when reporting crimes.
conflicts.side_b_position: City Manager's report favored officer discretion on vehicle consent searches (requiring written/recorded consent for homes and HEAT teams), semi-annual data reviews, and multi-agency dialogue before changing marijuana enforcement.
side_b_arguments: Requiring written forms during every patrol traffic stop raises situational control and officer safety considerations.
Meaningful changes to low-level drug enforcement require buy-in from the District Attorney, Sheriff, and District Court judges.
DPD has already begun Fair and Impartial Policing racial equity training and expanded data analytics.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote taken; City Manager Bonfield committed to returning for a comprehensive page-by-page work-session discussion on Thursday, September 4, 2014.

conflicts.issue: Length and Scope of Downtown Resident Parking Fee Phase-Out (Item 5)
conflicts.summary: Downtown residents, council members, and the City Attorney debated whether early downtown residents could retain free or discounted parking, how long a half-rate phase-in should last, and whether post-2008 residents could be excluded.
conflicts.side_a_position: Provide an extended multi-year half-price phase-in for current downtown residents (Don Moffitt initially favored 10 years, plus surface-lot rate relief; Coke Ariail/Kate Dobbs sought preservation of free parking).
side_a_arguments: Early downtown homeowners bought properties relying on city promises of free parking and helped revitalize downtown and grow property tax receipts (William 'Coke' Ariail, Kate Dobbs).

Charging full rates immediately asks ~130 downtown residents—who already pay higher downtown tax rates—for an extra $100,000/year, and Main Street residents prefer surface parking for safety (Don Moffitt).
conflicts.side_b_position: Limit subsidies to pre-2008 'pioneer' residents if legally possible, or keep the phase-out brief to avoid larger revenue losses.
side_b_arguments: Residents moving in after 2008 were aware of changing policies and should not receive the same long-term subsidy as the ~21 original pioneers (Steve Schewel).
Extending the 50% discount beyond three years costs the city approximately $50,000 in foregone revenue per additional year (clarified by Diane Catotti).
Legally, a retroactive 2008 cutoff would be arbitrary and capricious, leaving a uniform phase-out for all current residents as the only defensible option (City Attorney).
conflicts.resolution: Council compromised 6-0 on Don Moffitt's motion, seconded by Steve Schewel, adopting Option 2 with a five-year half-price phase-in for all current downtown residents through December 31, 2018.

conflicts.issue: Police Transparency, Racial Disparities in Traffic Stops, and Critical Incident Disclosures
conflicts.summary: During the third-quarter crime report, council members and residents debated how aggressively the Durham Police Department should release information and address racial profiling concerns amid pending SBI investigations.
conflicts.side_a_position: Demand faster public disclosure of critical incident facts and non-defensive reform of traffic-stop and policing practices.
side_a_arguments: Public confidence in police truthfulness and transparency requires timely answers on the Jesus Huerta, Derek Walker, and Jose Ocampo cases rather than months-long waits.
FADE's traffic-stop and search disparity statistics require open-minded review and concrete reforms.
Community activist Victoria Peterson called for replacing the Police Chief over homicides, lawsuits, and mental health crisis handling.
conflicts.side_b_position: Defend the Police Department's record while respecting independent SBI, Medical Examiner, and District Attorney investigative processes.
side_b_arguments: Part 1 crime is at a 14-year low and the vast majority of officers serve fairly without bias.
Underfunding of the SBI crime lab and Chief Medical Examiner delays limit what factual information the city can legally and ethically release before investigations conclude.
Chief Lopez urged community members to come forward with information on street violence rather than waiting solely on police.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote; council members expressed support for ongoing Human Relations Commission hearings and police internal review reforms while awaiting SBI findings.

conflicts.issue: Process and Transit Scoring Criteria for Dedicated Housing Funding Guidelines (Item 4)
conflicts.summary: Community member Stephen Hopkins and Mayor Bell objected to adopting new small-project and neighborhood revitalization scoring criteria without external public review, while Schewel requested adding half-mile transit-station bonus points.
conflicts.side_a_position: Continue adoption for two weeks to October 23 work session so staff can incorporate transit-proximity bonus points and solicit public comments.
side_a_arguments: No external housing stakeholders had reviewed the draft scoring criteria prior to the Council vote.
Incorporating Bo Glenn's last-minute suggestion for 4 bonus points near light rail stations warrants transparent public circulation via listserv.
A brief two-week delay will not derail late-December or early-January application timelines.
conflicts.side_b_position: Original staff recommendation sought immediate adoption to issue competitive application documents without delay before Assistant Director Larry Jarvis's departure.
side_b_arguments: Adopting guidelines promptly gives prospective developers adequate optioning and due diligence time ahead of late December/early January deadlines.
Staff followed the same internal drafting process used in prior funding cycles.
conflicts.resolution: Continued 6-0 to the October 23 work session with direction to add 4 transit-proximity bonus points and circulate the draft for public feedback.

conflicts.meeting_title: Durham City Council Work Session August 21, 2014
conflicts.issue: Written Consent for Vehicle Searches, Camera Mandates, CPRB Authority, and Marijuana Enforcement (HRC/CPRB Response)
conflicts.summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield's 131-page response and supporters (including FOP lodges and Hispanic community speakers) backed discretionary patrol vehicle consent searches and a measured review of DPD practices, whereas Council Members Steve Schewel and Cora Cole-McFadden and FADE/People's Alliance/NAACP/Durham CAN speakers demanded mandatory written vehicle search consent, stricter camera rules, independent CPRB authority, and immediate action on racial disparities.
conflicts.side_a_position: Require mandatory written consent forms for all vehicle consent searches, establish firmer camera activation rules, and pursue marijuana deprioritization and stronger civilian oversight.
side_a_arguments: Written consent is the most reliable safeguard against racial disparities in vehicle stops where dashcams/microphones cannot capture out-of-range encounters.
Wait-and-see data reviews until 2015 fail to stop ongoing harm, including 86% of simple marijuana arrests falling on African Americans.

Advocacy groups (FADE, SCSJ, People's Alliance, Durham CAN, NAACP, Durham Committee on the Affairs of Black People) warned that without mandatory written vehicle consent and CPRB investigative authority, systemic disparities will persist.
conflicts.side_b_position: Adopt the City Manager's recommendations requiring written/recorded consent only for home/premises and HEAT-team searches while preserving patrol officer discretion, and defend Chief Jose Lopez and DPD.
side_b_arguments: Requiring patrol officers to return to cruisers for paper forms during traffic stops creates officer safety and situational control risks.
DPD has already launched Fair and Impartial Policing training, expanded CIT training (180 officers), and strong data analytics.
Police union (FOP Lodge #2) and Hispanic speakers urged adopting Bonfield's report and opposed calls to remove Chief Lopez.
conflicts.resolution: No formal vote on the substance at the work session; Item 4 was placed on the September 2 General Business Agenda for Council deliberation.

conflicts.issue: Delaying vs. Enacting Revisions to the Roadside Solicitation (Panhandling) Ordinance (Item 3)
conflicts.summary: Public speakers and council members differed over whether to refer the revised roadside solicitation ordinance back to work session for additional residential-protection rules or enact it after a year of deliberation, as well as over the city's broader approach to panhandling.
conflicts.side_a_position: Move forward promptly with the consensus ordinance revision and allow regulated solicitation so impoverished residents are not further harmed by delays.
side_a_arguments: Stakeholders, police, the city attorney's office, and the Homeless Services Advisory Committee subcommittee spent over a year developing an alternative and reaching consensus.
Repeated postponements prolong hardship for individuals who rely on begging for sustenance (Carolyn Schul).
conflicts.side_b_position: Refer the ordinance back to work session to add residential protections and address ongoing neighborhood and business impacts rather than continuing to permit street begging.
side_b_arguments: Technical adjustments for driver-side solicitation on one-way streets were still unfinished, and Springfield, Missouri's rules protecting residents living near parks and intersections needed review (Bill Bell).
Large clusters of panhandlers along Fayetteville Street, Roxboro Road, and Alston Avenue hurt African-American business districts (Victoria Peterson).
Permitting solicitation fails to transform lives or end panhandling, and the city should pursue different strategies to connect people with resources (Cora Cole-McFadden).
conflicts.resolution: Council voted 6-0 to refer Item 3 to the Thursday work session for further review.

conflicts.issue: Item 10D (Severed): Substitute Motion Option 1 — Repeal $1.80/Month Solid Waste Fee & Adopt Commercial/Yard Waste Fee Schedules
conflicts.summary: At Mayor Bell's request, Item 10D was severed from the FY 2014-15 budget for an intense policy debate. Council Member Steve Schewel moved Option 1 to repeal the $1.80/month ($21.60/year) solid waste collection fee and replace its ~$1.4 million revenue with property taxes, joined by Diane Catotti and Don Moffitt, who argued the flat fee was regressive (hurting homeowners below ~$370,000 and renters who pay $0 directly under property tax) and would require a 56% hike next year to cover an $800,000 projected shortfall. Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden, Mayor Bill Bell, and Council Member Eugene Brown opposed repeal, arguing the solid waste enterprise fund already received $9.6 million in property tax subsidies, user fees akin to DATA bus fares were sound business practice, low-income residents had not complained, and adding ~0.6 cents to the tax rate risked giving Durham the highest municipal property tax rate in North Carolina. The substitute motion passed 4-3, with Bell, Brown, and Cole-McFadden voting no.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 4-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (4-3)

conflicts.issue: Excluding Wide Utility Easements from Tree Coverage Calculations (TC1300002)
conflicts.summary: Council and public speakers divided sharply over Horvath Associates' proposal to exclude utility easements of 50 feet or wider from tree-coverage calculations while still counting those easements toward residential density and impervious-surface allowances.
conflicts.side_a_position: Exclude wide utility easements (minus the first 50 feet) from gross tract area when calculating required tree coverage.
side_a_arguments: Power companies prohibit tree planting in wide transmission easements, forcing developers to set aside extra buildable acreage (e.g., 7.5 acres at Del Webb Carolina Arbors) to meet tree-coverage minimums.
Existing UDO exemptions already exclude ponds and road-widening rights-of-way where trees cannot be planted.
Preserving usable acreage lowers site development costs and improves housing affordability (Ron Horvath, Jared Edens, George Stancil).
conflicts.side_b_position: Reject or restrict the universal easement exemption so tree canopy is not reduced on large developments or near sensitive watersheds without parcel-level analysis.
side_b_arguments: Developers continue to receive full density and impervious-surface credit from the easement while shedding the corresponding tree-coverage obligation, harming air quality and raising urban temperatures (Will Wilson, Steve Schewel).
Staff had not mapped affected parcels near protected watersheds such as New Hope Creek, Ellerbe Creek, and the Eno River (Bob Healy, Pat Carstensen).
While small tracts encumbered by wide power easements might merit relief, there is no clear public interest in reducing tree requirements for very large developments (Steve Schewel).
conflicts.resolution: Unable to support the text amendment as drafted, Council voted 7-0 to reopen and continue the public hearing to May 19, 2014 so staff and the applicant could map affected parcels and model tract-size or percentage thresholds.

conflicts.issue: Continuum of Care / Homeless Funding Scoring Fairness and Transparency (Item 15)
conflicts.summary: During the Annual Action Plan public hearing, nonprofit leader Sharon Elliott-Bynum challenged the fairness and transparency of Community Development's Continuum of Care funding recommendations, prompting Council scrutiny despite staff explaining it was a separate process from CDBG/HOME/ESG.
conflicts.side_a_position: Investigate and reform funding recommendations to ensure fair scoring, process clarity, and inclusion of smaller/new nonprofits such as female veterans housing.
side_a_arguments: CAARE Inc.'s proposal to rehab a home for four homeless female veterans scored an average of 85 from the Citizens Advisory Committee compared to 84 for the staff-recommended agency, yet was passed over (Sharon Elliott-Bynum).
The recommended project was part two of a renewal rather than a new project, and an earlier $28,000 award from 2008-09 was never disbursed after the prior director's death (Sharon Elliott-Bynum).

Council must fully investigate the process at Thursday's work session because having the same organizations receive funding repeatedly does not appear fair (Cora Cole-McFadden; follow-up also requested by Bill Bell).
conflicts.side_b_position: Clarify that Continuum of Care recommendations follow a separate HUD process overseen by the Homeless Services Advisory Committee rather than the CDBG/HOME/ESG Annual Action Plan.
side_b_arguments: The funding cited by Ms. Bynum comes from the Continuum of Care process scheduled before the Homeless Services Advisory Committee, which makes recommendations separately from the Annual Action Plan hearing (Community Development Director Reginald Johnson).
Staff would research the historical $28,000 award question separately.
conflicts.resolution: Council voted 7-0 to receive all public hearing comments while directing Community Development staff to investigate Ms. Bynum's complaints and report back at Thursday's work session.

conflicts.issue: Item 38: Zoning Map Change — Harmony Road II Revisions (Z1400008)
conflicts.summary: Planner Steve Medlin and Standard Pacific attorney Patrick Byker presented Z1400008 to remove 2006 committed elements requiring an off-site asphalt trail connecting the 185-unit Chamberlain/Harmony Road II subdivision to the Woodcroft trail network and an on-site southern mulch trail, after Woodcroft's Community Association refused all proposed easements over a year of talks. Instead, Standard Pacific signed a private agreement with seven Chamberlain residents to spend the $75,000 trail budget (less rezoning/legal/consulting costs) on Chamberlain common-area recreation improvements. Council Member Don Moffitt reluctantly supported the change on grounds that off-site commitments should not be required, and Mayor Bell and Eugene Brown cited Woodcroft's refusal and Chamberlain neighbors' support. Council Members Diane Catotti and Steve Schewel dissented (5-2), arguing that decommitting the trail sacrificed a vital off-road Safe Route to Southwest Elementary School and future Third Fork Creek Trail connection.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 5-2)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (5-2)

conflicts.issue: Item 25: Zoning Map Change — Hope Valley Farms Pod BB Revisions (Z13-0012 / Murphy USA) (Initial Vote)
conflicts.summary: Planning staff presented Murphy USA's request on 6.77 acres at 1051 Martin Luther King Jr. Parkway to remove 2009 proffers barring fuel sales and convenience stores and to remove redundant roadway commitments already built by others. Attorneys Patrick Byker and Lewis Cheek emphasized a 0.8 opacity landscape buffer, 500-foot separation from the nearest townhomes, and $2 million in new tax base. Elm Grove Townhouse Association representative Aida Len O'Tougou requested a continuance because HOA board elections delayed neighborhood review, though Planning staff verified that first-class mail notices were sent to 45 nearby owners and the Elm Grove HOA in April. Following debate over notice and neighborhood compatibility, Council initially approved the rezoning 5-2 with Diane Catotti and Don Moffitt voting no.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Passed 5-2)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Passed (5-2)

conflicts.issue: Item 28: Resolution Approving Durham Traffic Separation Study (TSS) Recommendations
conflicts.summary: Dan Jewell, president of Durham Area Designers (DAD), addressed Item 28, urging Council to emphasize that the Durham Traffic Separation Study's limited scenarios were conceptual rather than recommended solutions and warning that some proposals could harm city livability unless subjected to immediate project-specific studies and public engagement. Council Member Steve Schewel argued against adopting the resolution—even with caveats—because accepting recommendations such as closing Dillard Street creates public expectations that those closures are settled policy, urging Council to merely receive the report instead. The motion to approve the resolution failed on a 3-3 tie vote with Diane Catotti absent.
conflicts.side_a_position: Voted Aye (Failed 3-3)
conflicts.side_b_position: Voted Nay / Opposed
conflicts.resolution: Failed (3-3)

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting October 20, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council unanimously adopted the Downtown Open Space Plan after extensive public support and approved a Neighborhood Stabilization Program 3 grant project ordinance for Southside infrastructure. In a 6-1 vote with Council Member Eugene Brown dissenting, the Council approved the $5.69 million acquisition of East Main Street, Elizabeth Street, Ramsey Street, and Hood Street properties for a new police headquarters and 911 communications complex despite concerns over cost, demolition of historic buildings, and urban design. The Council also approved the consent agenda and a pulled FY 2015 regional transportation modeling agreement with North Carolina State University.

agenda_items.title: Championship Proclamations and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell presented proclamations recognizing the 2014 NCAA national champion Duke University men's lacrosse and women's golf teams as well as the NCCU men's tennis HBCU national championship team. Council Member Diane Catotti also congratulated Durham dance pioneer Chuck Davis on receiving a Bessie Award in New York.

agenda_items.title: City Manager's Priority Items (Supplemental Items 20 and 21)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield introduced two supplemental items for addition to the evening's agenda: Item 20 regarding property acquisition for the proposed police headquarters on East Main Street and Item 21 for the Neighborhood Stabilization Program 3 grant project ordinance.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Item 7)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell read the headings of the consent agenda, covering minutes, a Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Commission appointment, FY14 carryover and FY15 budget/grant ordinances, CDBG contracts with Interfaith Hospitality Network and Urban Ministries of Durham, the City-County 911 interlocal agreement, and a stormwater repair contract amendment. Item 7 was pulled for separate discussion.

agenda_items.title: Downtown Open Space Plan Public Hearing and Adoption
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Tom Dawson of the Planning Department presented the three-year Downtown Open Space Plan, noting it is a non-binding policy guideline document for parks, plazas, and greenways recommended unanimously by the Planning Commission. Nine public speakers representing downtown residents, Triangle Land Conservancy, and Durham Area Designers urged adoption, while Council Members Diane Catotti and Steve Schewel emphasized retaining flexibility, developing future cost estimates, and protecting DPAC Green and the Beltline.

agenda_items.title: Proposed Property Acquisition for Police Headquarters (East Main / Elizabeth / Ramsey / Hood Streets)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: General Services Director Joel Reiser presented purchase options totaling $5.69 million for 4.439 acres from GWC Properties ($5.49 million) and 0.084 acres at 102 Hood Street from W.T. Wilkerson ($200,401) for a new police headquarters and 911 complex. Council Member Eugene Brown opposed the acquisition over its high per-acre cost, single appraisal, and ~$300,000-$400,000 demolition expense, while public speakers debated East Durham investment, total cost, and preservation of the 1928 and 1948 Carpenter Motor Company buildings.

agenda_items.title: Neighborhood Stabilization Program 3 (NSP3) Grant Project Ordinance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson presented a grant project ordinance to accept additional state-awarded NSP3 funds with a November 3 expenditure deadline to support infrastructure for the Southside redevelopment project.

agenda_items.title: FY 2015 Agreement with North Carolina State University for Triangle Regional Model
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Speaker James Chavis questioned why citizens had limited advance notice of the packet and asked whether the modeling contract connected to light rail and East Durham jobs. Mayor Bell clarified the contract covers regional transportation demand modeling rather than light rail construction and pledged community engagement, after which Council approved Item 7 and discussed establishing credibility criteria for future affordable housing market studies.

votes.item_title: Addition of City Manager's Priority Items (Items 20 and 21) to Agenda
votes.notes: Added supplemental Item 20 (Police Headquarters property acquisition) and Item 21 (NSP3 grant project ordinance).
votes.discussion_detail: City Manager Tom Bonfield requested the addition of two supplemental priority items to the October 20 agenda: Item 20 for the proposed acquisition of GWC Properties and W.T. Wilkerson parcels for a new police headquarters, and Item 21 for a Neighborhood Stabilization Program 3 grant project ordinance. No council member objected to adding the items. The Council voted 7-0 via the electronic voting system to add both items to the agenda.

votes.notes: Item 7 (NCSU Triangle Regional Model agreement) was pulled for separate discussion.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Bill Bell read through the consent agenda headings, including Council minutes, a Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Commission appointment, FY14 carryover and FY15 budget/grant ordinances, CDBG contracts for Interfaith Hospitality Network and Urban Ministries of Durham, the 911 interlocal agreement, and a stormwater infrastructure repair contract amendment. Item 7 was pulled from the consent docket for separate consideration. Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden moved approval of the remaining consent items, seconded by Council Member Diane Catotti, passing 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 15: Adoption of the Downtown Open Space Plan
votes.notes: Non-binding long-range policy guideline document; Council retains discretion over individual projects and funding.
votes.discussion_detail: Planning staff member Tom Dawson presented the Downtown Open Space Plan developed over three years with five public meetings and unanimous Planning Commission endorsement. Nine speakers, including Reynolds Smith, John Goebel, Chad Jemison of Triangle Land Conservancy, Dan Jewell of Durham Area Designers, Randolph Hester, and downtown residents, strongly urged adoption as a living, community-built plan. Council Member Diane Catotti requested future overall cost estimates and project prioritization while affirming council flexibility on individual sites, and Council Member Steve Schewel praised the Beltline, Convention Center Plaza, Church/Roxboro park, and DPAC Green concepts. After Eugene Brown called the question, the Council adopted the plan 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 20: Acquisition of East Main, Elizabeth, Ramsey, and Hood Street Properties for Police Headquarters
votes.notes: Purchase options of $5.49M (GWC Properties, 4.439 acres) and $200,401 (W.T. Wilkerson at 102 Hood St, 0.084 acres).
votes.discussion_detail: General Services Director Joel Reiser presented options to acquire 4.439 acres from GWC Properties for $5.49 million (appraised at $5.39 million, with 11 tenants providing 2015 lease revenue) and 0.084 acres at 102 Hood Street from W.T. Wilkerson for $200,401 (appraised at $80,000 for land/building alone, excluding ~$175,000 in annual net restaurant revenue). Mayor Bell questioned paying 2.5 times appraised value on Hood Street, and Council Member Eugene Brown criticized relying on a single appraisal and spending ~$1.33 million per acre plus $300,000-$400,000 in demolition costs (~$6 million total). Public commenters included GWC broker Marcus Jackson supporting the East Main location, Victoria Peterson opposing the $6 million outlay in favor of youth job training, and Rob Emerson opposing demolition of the historic 1928 and 1948 Carpenter Motor Company buildings. Council Members Diane Catotti, Don Moffitt, and Steve Schewel voted yes while requesting public urban design forums, walkable Main Street retail activation, and parking coordination with the Dillard light rail station; the motion passed 6-1 with Brown voting no.

votes.item_title: Item 21: Neighborhood Stabilization Program 3 (NSP3) Grant Project Ordinance
votes.notes: Accepts additional state-awarded NSP3 funds for Southside infrastructure with a November 3 expenditure deadline.
votes.discussion_detail: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson explained that the state awarded the City additional Neighborhood Stabilization Program 3 funds the previous week, subject to a strict November 3 expenditure deadline. The funds were designated for infrastructure improvements in the Southside redevelopment project. Without debate, the Council approved the grant project ordinance 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 7 (Pulled from Consent): FY 2015 Agreement with North Carolina State University for Triangle Regional Model
votes.notes: Following the vote, Mayor Bell questioned Community Development Director Reginald Johnson on establishing validation criteria for housing market studies, and Catotti explained the 10-day work session and 5-day agenda public notice timeline.
votes.discussion_detail: East Durham resident James Chavis pulled Item 7 to ask why citizens received late notice of large agenda packets and whether the NCSU agreement was tied to the light rail project and East Durham job opportunities. Mayor Bill Bell explained that the item was strictly a contract for the Triangle Regional Model transportation demand study rather than a light rail construction decision, while assuring Chavis of extensive public outreach as Triangle Transit moves forward. The Council then approved Item 7 by a 7-0 vote before Mayor Bell raised a follow-up question regarding validation criteria for credible housing market studies.

disagreements.issue: Acquisition of East Main Street / Carpenter Motor Company Site for New Police Headquarters
disagreements.summary: Council divided 6-1 over acquiring 4.523 acres along East Main Street for ~$5.69 million (plus demolition) for a new police headquarters and 911 complex, with Eugene Brown dissenting on cost and appraisal grounds while other members supported the site while pressing for urban design, retail activation, and historic/transit trade-offs.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the GWC Properties and W.T. Wilkerson land acquisition options to secure a consolidated central East Main Street site for police and 911 operations.
side_a_arguments: Extensive site search ruled out Fayetteville Street (planned for DHA redevelopment) and showed rebuilding on the existing site was cost-prohibitive.
Police and 911 departments wholeheartedly endorse the site, and GWC tenant rents during 2015 help offset the purchase premium over appraisal.
Staff committed to public design forums to improve Main Street walkability, streetscape, and potential public-private retail partnerships.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose the acquisition due to excessive cost (~$1.33M/acre plus demolition), reliance on a single appraisal, and paying 2.5x appraised value for the Hood Street parcel.
side_b_arguments: The city normally obtains two appraisals for major real estate acquisitions, whereas only one appraisal was done per property here.
Combined acquisition and $300,000-$400,000 demolition costs total roughly $6 million, representing an exceedingly high price per acre.
Public speakers also objected to demolishing the historic 1928 and 1948 Carpenter Motor Company buildings and questioned spending $6 million on a large headquarters.
disagreements.resolution: Approved 6-1; General Services proceeded with geotechnical/environmental due diligence and committed to public design forums and periodic Council updates.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting October 6, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council unanimously approved the Amanda Road street closing, the Hanover Point subdivision rezoning (reducing units from 68 to 41 despite neighbors' concerns over deteriorating state-maintained roads), and accepted public comments on the FY 2015-2020 Consolidated Plan needs hearing focused on transit-oriented affordable housing and homebuyer education. meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting August 4, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council voted 5-2—with Council Members Diane Catotti and Steve Schewel dissenting—to approve the Harmony Road II zoning revisions (Z1400008), removing 2006 trail-connection commitments to Woodcroft in exchange for a $75,000 Chamberlain neighborhood recreation fund after Woodcroft refused an off-site easement. Council unanimously approved UDO technical text amendments (TC1300001), the 2919 Fayetteville Street rezoning (Z1400003), the consent agenda, and a pulled neighborhood parking permit signage item (Item 31), and elected board appointees to the Cultural Advisory Board, Planning Commission, and Human Relations Commission by written ballot.

agenda_items.title: National Night Out Proclamation & Fill the Bus Campaign
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell presented a proclamation to Police Chief Jose Lopez recognizing the 31st annual National Night Out on August 5, 2014, followed by remarks on the 25-site Fill the Bus school supplies drive.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Adoption (Excluding Pulled Item 31)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council adopted the consent agenda excluding Item 31 (pulled by Eddie Davis and Linda Brown), including May 5 minutes, Homeless Services Advisory Committee appointment, June 2014 Crime Statistics Performance Audit, Verizon Wireless cell tower lease, Planning FY15 Work Program, NCSU stormwater retrofit project, Water Management on-call contracts, and the Downtown Loop waterline replacement contract.

agenda_items.title: Unified Development Ordinance Text Amendment — Technical Changes (TC1300001)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning's Michael Stock presented TC1300001 containing state/federal compliance updates, technical corrections, and clarifications to discretionary review standards (recommended 11-0 by the Planning Commission). With no public speakers, Council adopted the amendment 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change — 2919 Fayetteville Street (Z1400003)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planner Steve Medlin presented Z1400003 to rezone 1.409 acres between Fayetteville Street Elementary School and the American Tobacco Trail from Office-Institutional to Commercial Neighborhood (recommended 10-0 by the Planning Commission). With no public speakers, Council approved the rezoning 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change — Harmony Road II Revisions (Z1400008)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Standard Pacific (represented by Patrick Byker) requested removing 2006 committed elements requiring an off-site asphalt trail to Woodcroft and an on-site mulch trail because Woodcroft Community Association refused an easement, proposing instead a $75,000 Chamberlain recreation fund (net of legal/rezoning costs). Council Members Diane Catotti and Steve Schewel voted no to protect greenway connectivity and Safe Routes to School, while the 5-member majority approved the revisions citing Woodcroft's refusal and Chamberlain residents' support.

agenda_items.title: Pulled Consent Item: Residential Permit Parking Signage (Linda Brown)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Resident Linda Brown opposed annual city parking decals and sign restrictions affecting residents with steep driveways and student relatives; Council Members Steve Schewel and Diane Catotti noted she had withdrawn her opposition at the prior work session and Council approved the item 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Ballot Appointments: Cultural Advisory Board, Planning Commission, and Human Relations Commission
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Following public comment from Rafiq Zaidi on the Human Relations Commission appointment and Mayor Bell's defense of reappointing members with near-100% attendance, the City Clerk announced the ballot winners: Tess O'Connor (Cultural Advisory Board, 5 votes), Brian Buzby (Planning Commission, 5 votes), and Diane Standaert (Human Relations Commission, 4 votes).

votes.item_title: Consent Agenda Adoption (excluding pulled Item 31)
votes.notes: Item 31 was pulled by Council Member Eddie Davis and speaker Linda Brown.
votes.discussion_detail: Mayor Bill Bell read through the consent agenda items, including May 5, 2014 minutes, Homeless Services Advisory Committee appointment, June 2014 Crime Statistics Performance Audit, Verizon Wireless cell tower lease, Planning Department FY 2015 Work Program, NCSU stormwater retrofit project, Water Management on-call master service agreements, and the Downtown Loop waterline replacement contract with J.F. Wilkerson Contracting Company. Item 31 was pulled for separate discussion. The remaining consent agenda passed 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 36: Unified Development Ordinance Text Amendment — Technical Changes (TC1300001)
votes.notes: Recommended 11-0 by the Planning Commission on May 13, 2014.
votes.discussion_detail: Michael Stock of the Planning Department presented UDO text amendment TC1300001, grouping technical changes into three categories: state/federal compliance updates, technical corrections and codifications, and clarifications to discretionary review standards previously adopted under TC1100007. The Planning Commission had recommended approval 11-0. With no council questions and no public speakers, Council closed the hearing and approved TC1300001 by a 7-0 vote.

votes.item_title: Item 37: Zoning Map Change — 2919 Fayetteville Street (Z1400003)
votes.notes: Rezones 1.409 acres from Office-Institutional to Commercial Neighborhood; recommended 10-0 by Planning Commission on June 10, 2014.
votes.discussion_detail: Planner Steve Medlin presented Z1400003, a request to rezone 1.409 acres at 2919 Fayetteville Street between Fayetteville Street Elementary School and the American Tobacco Trail from Office-Institutional to Commercial Neighborhood without an attached development plan, to allow retail uses such as a laundromat. votes.notes: Removes 2006 committed elements for off-site Woodcroft asphalt trail and on-site mulch trail while modifying timing triggers on remaining commitments.

Instead, Standard Pacific signed a private agreement with seven Chamberlain residents to spend the $75,000 trail budget (less rezoning/legal/consulting costs) on Chamberlain common-area recreation improvements. Council Member Don Moffitt reluctantly supported the change on grounds that off-site commitments should not be required, and Mayor Bell and Eugene Brown cited Woodcroft's refusal and Chamberlain neighbors' support. Council Members Diane Catotti and Steve Schewel dissented (5-2), arguing that decommitting the trail sacrificed a vital off-road Safe Route to Southwest Elementary School and future Third Fork Creek Trail connection.

votes.notes: Pulled by Council Member Eddie Davis and speaker Linda Brown.

votes.notes: Written ballot results read by City Clerk: Tess O'Connor (5 votes, Cultural Advisory Board); Brian Buzby (5 votes, Planning Commission); Diane Standaert (4 votes, Human Relations Commission). Clerk confirmed the ballots themselves constituted the formal vote.
votes.discussion_detail: Council members completed written ballots earlier in the meeting for vacancies on the Durham Cultural Advisory Board, Durham Planning Commission, and Human Relations Commission. Prior to the tally announcement, speaker Rafiq Zaidi commented on the Human Relations Commission appointment, and Mayor Bill Bell explained on the record that he voted to reappoint the incumbent (Diane Standaert) because she was eligible for a second term and had nearly 100% attendance rather than because of her policy stance. The City Clerk announced the winning totals—Tess O'Connor (5 votes), Brian Buzby (5 votes), and Diane Standaert (4 votes)—and confirmed no separate roll-call motion was required.

disagreements.issue: Decommitting Trail Connections in Harmony Road II / Chamberlain Subdivision (Z1400008)
disagreements.summary: Council split 5-2 over whether to release Standard Pacific from a 2006 committed element to build an asphalt trail connecting Chamberlain to Woodcroft's trail system and a southern mulch trail.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve removing the trail commitments because Woodcroft refused an off-site easement and Chamberlain residents negotiated a $75,000 recreation fund compromise.
side_a_arguments: Woodcroft Community Association formally rejected four to six proposed alignments across its private property.
Chamberlain residents agreed to redirect the $75,000 trail budget (net of legal/consulting costs) toward neighborhood recreation amenities.
Existing zoning lacked a timing trigger, and off-site easements beyond a developer's property boundary should not be enforced.
disagreements.side_b_position: Oppose decommitting the trails in order to preserve critical off-road pedestrian/bicycle connectivity to Southwest Elementary School and the Third Fork Creek Trail.
side_b_arguments: BPAC and residents rely on off-road trail links rather than forcing children onto city streets.
Removing the developer's commitment pushes the eventual cost of completing the Third Fork Creek tributary trail onto city taxpayers.
Woodcroft itself benefited from visionary trails, and the developer should pursue another alignment (such as toward Brindhurst/Tall Oaks) or mediation.
disagreements.resolution: Approved 5-2 (Catotti and Schewel voting no), removing the trail commitments.

meetings.title: CityLife: New City Budget & Resident Impacts (July 2014)
meetings.executive_summary: In this CityLife television broadcast hosted by Beverly Thompson, Council Member Steve Schewel and City Manager Tom Bonfield explained the newly adopted $390 million FY 2014-15 City of Durham budget and its impacts on residents. They discussed the 2.37-cent property tax rate increase (including debt service, the half-cent parks maintenance allocation, and the 4-3 repeal of the $1.80/month solid waste fee), capital investments in Twin Lakes and Herndon parks, increased street resurfacing funding, and state privilege license tax revenue losses.

agenda_items.title: Parks CIP, Street Resurfacing, Historic Districts, and School Resource Officers
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Schewel and Bonfield highlighted parks capital projects (Twin Lakes resurfacing, Herndon Road Park turf, American Tobacco Trail parking, tennis/basketball courts), increasing annual street resurfacing from $750,000 to $1 million, $20,000 in reserves for Golden Belt area historic district planning, and interagency talks with Durham Public Schools and the County over school resource officer funding.

agenda_items.title: Youth Pathways (Made in Durham / MDC), Yard Waste Fee, Privilege License Tax Loss, and Peer City Tax Comparison

General Assembly's repeal of the local privilege license tax ($129,000 impact in FY15 and $2.9 million projected next year) and argued that under a combined tax-and-fee cost-per-customer analysis, Durham sits in the middle of peer cities.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting June 16, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: In a pivotal budget meeting, the Durham City Council voted 4-3 on a substitute motion by Steve Schewel (with Bell, Brown, and Cole-McFadden dissenting) to repeal the $1.80/month solid waste collection fee and replace it with a property tax increase, and then adopted the remaining FY 2014-15 budget and CIP ordinances 6-1 (with Eugene Brown dissenting over the final budget's inclusion of the fee repeal). agenda_items.title: Parks & Recreation Month, DPD Forensics ISO Accreditation, Linda Bratcher Retirement, and Council Announcements
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell presented resolutions for Parks and Recreation Month and the Durham Police Department Forensics Services Division's ISO/IEC 17025 accreditation. Council members also recognized retiring staff member Linda Bratcher and praised Steve Schewel's Durham News op-ed on city taxes.

agenda_items.title: City Manager's Priority Items (Item 33 Order, Supplemental Item 36, and HRC/CPRB Memo)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield moved Item 33 after Item 32, added supplemental Item 36 (Riverside on the Eno CIP ordinance amendment), and added his review/timeline memo on the Human Relations Commission and Civilian Police Review Board recommendations to the public record.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda Adoption (Excluding Pulled Items 10 and 11)

disagreements.issue: Repeal of the $1.80/Month Solid Waste Collection Fee vs. Property Tax Replacement (Item 10D & Final Budget)
disagreements.summary: Council divided 4-3 on repealing the $1.80/month solid waste collection fee and replacing its $1.4 million revenue with property taxes, leading Eugene Brown to vote no (6-1) on the final overall budget.
disagreements.side_a_position: Repeal the flat $1.80/month ($21.60/year) solid waste fee and fund the $1.4 million through the property tax rate.
side_a_arguments: A flat per-household fee is regressive, charging a $75,000 homeowner or low-income renter the same $21.60/year as a $500,000 homeowner.
Any homeowner below ~$370,000 in assessed value—and single-family/duplex renters who pay $0 directly under property tax—pays less under Option 1.
Keeping the fee would require a 56% fee hike next year to cover a projected $800,000 solid waste shortfall.
disagreements.side_b_position: Retain the $1.80/month solid waste user fee to stabilize the solid waste enterprise fund and avoid raising property taxes.
side_b_arguments: The $20 million solid waste fund already receives $9.6 million in general-fund property tax subsidies from all property owners, including businesses and multi-family residents without city pickup.
Like DATA bus fares, a modest $1.80/month user fee for households receiving collection service is not regressive, and DSS assistance covers hardship cases.
Replacing the fee plus county/other increases risks giving Durham the highest municipal property tax rate among North Carolina's largest cities, hurting competitiveness.
disagreements.resolution: Option 1 repeal passed 4-3; the remaining FY 2014-15 budget ordinances then passed 6-1 with Eugene Brown dissenting because the final budget incorporated the fee repeal.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting June 2, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: With Council Member Diane Catotti absent, the Durham City Council rejected a resolution approving recommendations of the Durham Traffic Separation Study (TSS) on a 3-3 tie vote after Steve Schewel objected to proposals such as closing Dillard Street, then voted 6-0 merely to receive the TSS report. disagreements.summary: Council tied 3-3 on adopting a resolution accepting the Durham Traffic Separation Study recommendations, then voted 6-0 merely to receive the report without endorsing its conceptual street closures.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the staff-recommended resolution accepting the TSS report with caveats requiring future project-specific studies and public input.

meetings.title: Proposed Budget for Fiscal Year 2014-2015 for City of Durham, North Carolina
meetings.executive_summary: This video captures City Manager Tom Bonfield's formal presentation of the proposed $386.7 million Fiscal Year 2014-2015 City of Durham budget and FY 2015-2020 Capital Improvement Plan to Mayor Bill Bell and the City Council. agenda_items.discussion_summary: Paul Wiebke of Public Works presented a proposed 7.5% stormwater rate increase effective July 1, 2014, to fund stormwater retrofit capital projects required under Falls Lake Stage 1 existing development rules and NPDES permit compliance. Wiebke noted the 7.5% increase was 1% lower than projected the prior year and would raise annual bills by $2.76 (Tier 1), $5.64 (Tier 2), and $11.28 (Tier 3) for residential customers and roughly $110 for non-residential customers. No members of the public spoke.

agenda_items.title: Network Hut License Agreement between the City of Durham and Google
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Victoria Peterson pulled Consent Item 2, welcoming Google Fiber to Durham while raising concerns that city property sites were not yet specified and urging the city to ensure local hiring—including for more than 200 locally trained copper and fiber workers who often face employment barriers due to criminal records. votes.item_title: Consent Agenda (Items 1, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, excluding pulled Item 2)

votes.item_title: Item 12: UDO Text Amendment – Tree Coverage Calculations (TC13-00002) Referral Back to Administration

Alexander Drive and US Highway 70, reporting adequate water/sewer capacity and a positive fiscal impact analysis for up to 141 single-family homes or a place of worship, while noting the applicant anticipated seeking higher-density rezoning later. votes.item_title: Item 14: UDO Text Amendment – Watershed Protection Overlay, Rural Village (TC13-00003)

Because Rougemont lies entirely within Durham County's jurisdiction, there was no direct impact inside city limits, and the amendment was needed solely to keep the city and county versions of the joint UDO consistent after unanimous County approval and a 12-0 Planning Commission recommendation on February 11, 2014. No council members asked questions and no members of the public spoke during the hearing. Council closed the public hearing and approved the text amendment 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 15: Adoption of Proposed Stormwater Rates for FY 2015 (7.5% Increase)
votes.notes: Effective July 1, 2014; funds Falls Lake Stage 1 stormwater retrofits and NPDES compliance.
