meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting May 5, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Bill Bell and all six City Council members met on May 5, 2014, adopting the consent agenda and holding public hearings on the FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan for federal HUD and local dedicated housing funds, prior-year HUD grant reconciliations, inspections permit fee updates, the UDI Farm comprehensive plan amendment and RS-20 rezoning (approved 6-0 with Mayor Bell recused due to his employment at UDI CDC), and a street closing adjacent to Lakewood Elementary School. Council also heard extensive testimony from Housing for New Hope clients, Urban Ministries, Durham Community Land Trustees, and the Citizens Advisory Committee during the Annual Action Plan hearing, and reviewed the Durham Police Department's Q1 2014 crime report showing a 36% spike in Part 1 violent crime driven by multi-victim shootings alongside the launch of a juvenile misdemeanor diversion program.

agenda_items.title: Proclamations, Council Comments, and City Manager Priority Agenda Adjustments
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell and Councilmember Steve Schewel presented proclamations for Children's Mental Health Awareness Week, Police Week, Workforce Development Professionals Month, National Drinking Water Week (with student poster contest winners), Older Americans Month, and Fitzgerald Family Day honoring Robert George Fitzgerald and the Pauli Murray Project. Councilmembers Eugene Brown and Cora Cole-McFadden recognized public employees for Public Service Recognition Week, and Mayor Bell promoted an upcoming WNCU radio forum on the Southside neighborhood revitalization. City Manager Tom Bonfield requested holding Consent Item 7 (CASA HOME funds) until after Item 26 and adding Supplemental Item 31 (Q1 Public Safety Report), while Mayor Pro Tem Cole-McFadden flagged a follow-up question on Item 6 regarding how Connecting Youth verifies participants are Durham County residents.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Connecting Youth, Swimming Pool Study, Fire Station 9, Transit-Oriented Housing Resolution, 5-Year Housing Plan)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council approved the consent agenda excluding Item 7, covering minutes, a TDA appointment, street acceptances, the Connecting Youth MOA (Item 6), bid reports, a swimming pool facilities assessment study with Sasaki Design, Leigh Farm Park design amendment #4, 411 Cleveland St roof renovations, Fire Station 9 design/testing amendments, a resolution supporting affordable housing around transit stations, street/sidewalk/waterline contracts, a yard waste facility contract amendment, an update to the five-year comprehensive housing strategy and dedicated funding plan, and UNRBA Falls Lake Stage 2 support.

agenda_items.title: Draft FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan for CDBG, HOME, and ESG Funds
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Community Development Director Reginald Johnson and Federal Programs Coordinator Wilma Conyers presented the FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan allocating $1,795,508 in CDBG, $831,909 in HOME, and $147,357 in ESG funds, alongside local dedicated housing penny funds. Housing for New Hope staff, Rapid Rehousing clients (including the Glasper family), Urban Ministries, Durham Community Land Trustees, and Citizens Advisory Committee members testified in support of rapid rehousing and rental preservation. Councilmembers Diane Catotti and Steve Schewel questioned $192,000 in gap financing for Vermillion while praising a shift raising Habitat for Humanity second-mortgage assistance in Northeast Central Durham from $120,000 to $180,000; Council voted 7-0 to receive comments and then 7-0 to adopt the plan.

agenda_items.title: Amendments to FY 2011-2014 Annual Action Plans and CASA HOME Funds Award
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Wilma Conyers presented formal amendments reconciling $244,750 in HOME funds, $74,000 in CDBG funds, and $11,082 in ESG funds across FY 2011-2012, 2012-2013, and 2013-2014 Annual Action Plans to align with the general ledger and meet federal expenditure deadlines. With no public speakers, Council approved Item 26 unanimously 7-0 and immediately thereafter approved Consent Item 7 awarding HOME funds to Community Alternatives for Supportive Abodes (CASA) for permanent affordable housing 7-0.

agenda_items.title: Amendment to City-County Inspections Permit Fee Ordinance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City-County Inspections Director Jean Bradham presented targeted updates to the permit fee schedule, which had not been comprehensively adjusted since July 2011. The proposal left new single-family and new commercial permit fees unchanged while introducing a progressive plan-review resubmittal fee for uncorrected deficiencies, a first-reinspection fee for HVAC equipment replacements, and minor category fee increases and clarifications to recover inspection costs in line with peer cities. No members of the public spoke.

agenda_items.title: Comprehensive Plan Amendment – UDI Farm (A14-00001)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell recused himself from Items 28 and 29 as an employee of UDI CDC, turning the chair over to Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden. Pat Young presented UDI CDC's request to change the future land use map designation of 2.6 acres of a 5.9-acre site at 4601 Industry Lane from Office to Low Density Residential to permit urban agriculture and aquaponics (recommended 12-1 by the Planning Commission). Applicant attorney Patrick Byker explained that floodplain conditions prevented viable office development despite years of marketing.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change – UDI Farm (Z14-00001)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: With Mayor Pro Tem Cole-McFadden presiding, Pat Young presented UDI CDC's rezoning of 5.9 acres at 4601 Industry Lane from Office and Institutional (OI) to Residential Suburban 20 (RS-20) to allow an EDA-grant-funded commercial vegetable farm and aquaponics facility (recommended 12-1 by the Planning Commission). Attorney Patrick Byker, aquaponics specialist Kevin Hammock, and UDI President Ed Stewart answered council questions from Steve Schewel, Diane Catotti, and Don Moffitt regarding fish species (tilapia and perch), closed-loop water recycling and rainwater capture, 50-foot agricultural setbacks, odor absence, and projections to create 40 jobs over three years.

agenda_items.title: Street Closing – 127-Linear-Foot Right-of-Way Segment West of Chapel Hill Road (SC13-0006)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young presented Case SC13-0006, a request by Beall's Design and Construction to close a 127-linear-foot right-of-way segment just west of Chapel Hill Road bordered by the applicant's property and Lakewood Elementary School, recombining 50% of the closed right-of-way to the applicant and 50% to Durham Public Schools. John Blakely of Edens Land Corp appeared on behalf of the applicant with no opposition from the public.

agenda_items.title: Police Department 2014 First Quarter Summary Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief Jose Lopez reported a 36% increase in Part 1 violent crime (driven by 176 aggravated assault incidents involving 254 victims from multi-victim shootings into occupied dwellings and crowds), a 10% rise in property crime (burglaries and larcenies), a 13% rise in overall Part 1 index crime compared to Q1 2013's 14-year low, and slower priority-1 response times (6.1 minutes vs. 5.8-minute target), alongside drops in rape and auto theft and launch of the County Misdemeanor Diversion Program for 16- and 17-year-olds. Mayor Bell called the quarter a 'bad start' and requested individual offender counts behind the 304 juvenile offenses; Councilmembers Eddie Davis and Cora Cole-McFadden pressed Lopez on lack of diversity in the current police academy class and above-state academy requirements, while Steve Schewel, Eugene Brown, and Don Moffitt questioned violent crime tactics and diversion training.

votes.item_title: City Manager Priority Items (Hold Item 7 Until After Item 26; Add Supplemental Item 31)
votes.notes: Mayor Pro Tem Cole-McFadden asked a follow-up question on Item 6 (Connecting Youth Durham County residency verification) without pulling the item.
votes.discussion_detail: City Manager Tom Bonfield presented two priority agenda adjustments: holding Consent Item 7 (award of HOME funds to Community Alternatives for Supportive Abodes for permanent affordable housing) until after public hearing Item 26, and adding Supplemental Item 31 (Police Department 2014 Q1 Public Safety Report) to the agenda. Before voting, Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden clarified she did not wish to pull Consent Item 6 (Connecting Youth MOA) but asked whether the manager had followed up on how the program verifies that participating youth are Durham County residents; Bonfield replied he had inquired but did not yet have an answer. Council then voted 7-0 to approve the priority agenda adjustments.

votes.item_title: Item 25 (Part 1): Close Public Hearing and Receive Citizen Comments on Draft FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan
votes.notes: Initial motion received public hearing comments; Council immediately took a second vote to formally adopt the plan.
votes.discussion_detail: After staff presented the draft FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan ($1.795M CDBG, $831.9K HOME, $147.4K ESG), seven speakers testified in support of rapid rehousing and rental preservation, including Housing for New Hope staff, previously homeless clients Tara and Demar Glasper, Durham Community Land Trustees director Selena Mack ($300,000 for 30 West End units), Citizens Advisory Committee member Shameka Rhinehart, Urban Ministries' Alexander Herring, and Frank Moore. Councilmembers Cole-McFadden, Moffitt, Catotti, Schewel, and Bell praised the shift increasing Habitat for Humanity second-mortgage funding in Northeast Central Durham from $120,000 to $180,000 (adding roughly four net units), while Catotti and Schewel raised concerns about $192,000 in gap financing for Vermillion and asked for deeper review when it returns individually. Council first voted 7-0 to receive the public hearing comments.

votes.item_title: Item 25 (Part 2): Adopt FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan for CDBG, HOME, and ESG Funds
votes.notes: Required formal adoption vote after staff reminded Council the first vote only received comments; due to HUD by May 15.
votes.discussion_detail: Immediately after Council voted to receive public comments on Item 25, staff reminded Mayor Bell and Council that formal adoption of the FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan was required for submission to HUD by the May 15 deadline. Staff confirmed that the adopted plan incorporated the May 1 supplemental memo adjusting the chart to increase homebuyer assistance from $120,000 to $180,000 to support at least nine Habitat for Humanity homebuyers in Northeast Central Durham, and that individual projects such as Vermillion would return separately for Council approval. Council moved, seconded, and unanimously adopted the Annual Action Plan 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 26: Amendments to FY 2011-2012, 2012-2013, and 2013-2014 Annual Action Plans
votes.notes: Reconciles $244,750 in HOME, $74,000 in CDBG, and $11,082 in ESG funds to the general ledger.
votes.discussion_detail: Federal Programs Coordinator Wilma Conyers presented proposed amendments to the FY 2011-2012, 2012-2013, and 2013-2014 Annual Action Plans reconciling $244,750 in HOME funds, $74,000 in CDBG funds, and $11,082 in ESG funds to the city's general ledger in order to meet federal expenditure deadlines. Conyers certified newspaper, listserv, library, City Hall, and website public notice from April 4 through May 5. No council questions were raised and no members of the public spoke during the hearing. Council closed the public hearing and approved the amendments 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 7 (Deferred Consent): Award of HOME Funds to Community Alternatives for Supportive Abodes (CASA) for Permanent Affordable Housing
votes.notes: Taken up immediately after approval of Item 26 per City Manager's priority request.
votes.discussion_detail: Following the approval of prior-year HUD grant reconciliations in Item 26, Mayor Bell brought forward Consent Item 7, which awarded HOME funds to Community Alternatives for Supportive Abodes (CASA) for permanent affordable housing. The City Manager had asked Council to hold the item until after the Item 26 public hearing was completed. With no additional discussion needed, Council moved, seconded, and passed Item 7 unanimously 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 27: Amendment to City-County Inspections Permit Fee Ordinance
votes.notes: Adds progressive plan-review resubmittal fee and first-reinspection fee for HVAC replacements; leaves new single-family and commercial permits unchanged.
votes.discussion_detail: City-County Inspections Director Jean Bradham presented targeted updates to the inspections permit fee ordinance, noting that new single-family residential and new commercial permit fees were unchanged. The amendments added a progressive fee for repeated plan reviews when applicants fail to correct noted deficiencies, added a reinspection fee on first reinspections of HVAC equipment replacements to encourage first-time compliance, and adjusted select trade permit fees to recover inspection costs in line with peer cities. Bradham confirmed outreach to homebuilders, general contractors, and mechanical/plumbing contractors. With no public speakers or council objections, Council closed the hearing and approved the ordinance 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 28: Comprehensive Plan Amendment – UDI Farm (Case A14-00001)
votes.notes: Mayor Bill Bell recused himself and abstained as an employee of applicant UDI CDC; Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden presided.

votes.discussion_detail: With Mayor Pro Tem Cole-McFadden presiding and Mayor Bell recused, Pat Young presented Case Z14-00001 rezoning approximately 5.9 acres at 4601 Industry Lane from Office and Institutional (OI) to Residential Suburban 20 (RS-20) to permit an aquaponics and commercial vegetable farming project funded by a federal Economic Development Administration grant (recommended 12-1 by the Planning Commission). votes.discussion_detail: Pat Young presented Case SC13-0006, a street-closing petition by Beall's Design and Construction for a 127-linear-foot right-of-way segment just west of Chapel Hill Road bordered by the applicant's property and Lakewood Elementary School on the north side. Upon closing, the right-of-way would be recombined equally, 50% to the applicant and 50% to Durham Public Schools. meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting April 21, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: Mayor Bill Bell and all six City Council members met on April 21, 2014, approving the consent agenda (excluding pulled Item 7), extending an incentive deadline for The Gentian Group's Hotel Durham project, and voting 6-1—over Mayor Bell's dissent—to approve a $3.97 million, 15-year economic development incentive agreement with Austin Lawrence Partners East for the 26-story City Center tower and Jack Tar Motel redevelopment. Bell argued the contract should guarantee a minimum annual property tax yield of $327,400, while the council majority and legal/finance staff warned that tying payments directly to tax yields risked violating state constitutional prohibitions on tax rebates and could jeopardize project financing. Council also unanimously approved targeted revisions to the Economic Development Policy enabling Ninth Street corridor grants after Schewel and Bell flagged broader policy reforms for a future city-county overhaul, approved the pulled MCNC telecommunications license agreement 7-0, and excused two work-session absences.

agenda_items.title: Earth Day, Mayor's Water Conservation Challenge, and National Community Development Week Proclamations
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell presented proclamations for Earth Day (accepted by Parks and Recreation Director Rhonda Parker), the Wyland Foundation National Mayor's Challenge for Water Conservation (with Water Management Assistant Director Vicki Westbrook noting Durham ranked 9th nationally among peer cities), and National Community Development Week marking 40 years of CDBG and 24 years of HOME programs (accepted by Reginald Johnson). Mayor Pro Tem Cora Cole-McFadden also recognized Carolina Theatre staff attending ahead of their consent agenda services agreement.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (DCLT Southside Funds, Carolina Theatre Agreement, TIGER Grant, Sidewalks & Infrastructure)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Council approved the consent agenda with the exception of Item 7 (MCNC telecommunications license agreement), which was pulled by Victoria Peterson. Approved items included minutes, a Workforce Development Board appointment, dedicated housing and HOME funds for Durham Community Land Trustees in Southside, a partial payment to Parkwood Volunteer Fire Department, an 800 MHz radio agreement with Fayetteville, the Carolina Theatre building and services agreement, CFP development reimbursement amendments, a sidewalk grant agreement on Campus Walk Avenue and LaSalle Street, BPAC and Recreation Advisory Commission annual reports, sewer pipe/manhole rehabilitation contract SR-58, and a FY 2014 TIGER planning grant application.

agenda_items.title: Amendment to Economic Incentive Contract with The Gentian Group LLC (Hotel Durham / Holland Hotel)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Thomas Leathers of OEWD presented an amendment extending Section 3.1.1's deadline to secure a final certificate of compliance to November 30 following delays caused by earlier right-of-way and easement public hearings. Councilmember Steve Schewel sought clarification on the $400,000 inspections certificate figure, and Leathers confirmed it reflected good-faith expenditures already made by the developer and created no additional city liability until the project is completed. No members of the public spoke.

agenda_items.title: Economic Development Incentive Agreement with Austin Lawrence Partners East, LLC (City Center & Jack Tar)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Kevin Dick, developer Greg Hills, and HITT Contracting's Amanda Moreau presented the $85 million ($65 million qualified capital investment) redevelopment featuring a 26-story mixed-use tower at 119 W. Parrish St., restoration of five historic facades on Parrish and Main Streets, and renovation of the Jack Tar Motel and 260-space parking deck at 202 N. Corcoran St., backed by up to $3.97 million in city incentives over 15 years and 15% Durham-based / 5% SDBE contracting goals. Downtown Durham Inc., DCVB, the Chamber, the Institute of Minority Economic Development, and Pizzeria Toro spoke in support, while Council questioned facade bracing, Duke office relocation vs. new jobs, financing via a Virginia REIT, condo vs. rental flexibility, and construction disruption. Mayor Bell opposed approving the contract without language guaranteeing at least $327,400 in annual general fund property taxes across future revaluations and asked to hold the vote until Thursday, but the council majority called the question and approved the agreement 6-1.

agenda_items.title: Proposed Revisions to Economic Development Incentive Policy (Ninth Street Corridor & Grant Updates)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Reginald Jones of OEWD presented targeted updates adding the Ninth Street commercial corridor as an incentive target area beyond the CDA, setting a $50,000 private investment floor for non-downtown CDA building grants, merging sign/facade grants into retail/professional services grants up to $20,000, extending completion timelines from 12 to 18 months, and renaming the urban growth area. Victoria Peterson urged greater African American downtown property ownership and African sister-city ties (Mayor Bell noted Arusha, Tanzania). Steve Schewel and Mayor Bell raised broad policy reforms for the upcoming joint city-county overhaul—including lowering the 16% incentive cap, tying job incentives to Durham residents, requiring 60% AMI affordable housing bonuses, and ending non-city capital incentives—and agreed to approve the narrow Ninth Street revisions 7-0 after staff warned deferral would stall Ninth Street merchant grants.

agenda_items.title: Telecommunications License Agreement with Microelectronics Center of North Carolina (MCNC)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Victoria Peterson pulled Consent Item 7 to publicly thank MCNC for hiring Durham residents with criminal records and challenging backgrounds in past copper and fiber optic installations, urging the city to encourage other fiber providers to adopt similar second-chance hiring practices. disagreements.issue: Austin Lawrence Partners (City Center / Jack Tar) Incentive Agreement – Minimum Guaranteed Property Tax Yield vs. Capital Investment Metric
disagreements.summary: Mayor Bill Bell dissented in a 6-1 vote on the $3.97 million, 15-year incentive agreement for the City Center tower and Jack Tar Motel redevelopment, insisting the contract include an absolute minimum annual property tax yield ($327,400) rather than relying solely on capital investment thresholds, while the six council members and city finance/legal staff supported approving the agreement as drafted under existing policy.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the $3.97M incentive agreement immediately as drafted under existing economic development policy, relying on conservative tax assessor estimates ($60.9M assessed value) and avoiding constitutional tax-rebate risks.
side_a_arguments: Existing city policy bases incentives on qualified capital investment ($65M minimum) rather than actual tax revenue yields because directly linking incentives to tax revenues or requiring make-up payments risks violating the North Carolina Constitution's prohibition on tax rebates.

Finance staff already applied conservative buffers by basing projections on the tax assessor's $60.9M valuation (about 10% below the $65M minimum investment), capping the incentive at ~80.9% of projected property tax, and excluding ~$3.4M in projected hotel occupancy and sales taxes.
Delaying approval past April would disrupt the developer's imminent REIT financing term sheet and push back demolition and construction timelines.
disagreements.side_b_position: Hold the agreement until Thursday and amend Section 2.1 (or attach Exhibit D) to guarantee that the project generates at least $327,400 annually in general fund property tax revenue regardless of future property revaluations.
side_b_arguments: While the city's 15-year payout (~$265K/year) is fixed in dollars, future countywide property revaluations typically lower tax rates and could erode actual property tax inflows below the $327,400 projection.

Future councils paying out general fund dollars over 15 years should have contractual certainty of the minimum property tax revenue returning to the general fund rather than relying on non-binding memos or uncertain sales/hotel taxes.
disagreements.resolution: Council rejected Mayor Bell's request to hold the item until Thursday and approved the incentive agreement 6-1, with Bell voting No; City Attorney Fred Lamar agreed to examine revenue-guarantee mechanisms during the upcoming comprehensive Economic Development Policy overhaul.

disagreements.issue: FY 2014-2015 Budget Guidelines – Scope and Tax Level of Dedicated Parks Funding ('Penny for Parks')
disagreements.summary: Council debated whether dedicated property tax funding for parks should be used for new facilities and land expansion or restricted strictly to maintenance and renovation of existing assets, and weighed tax/fee burdens on lower-income residents before settling on an informational study capped at 1 cent solely for maintenance and renovation.
disagreements.side_a_position: Limit any dedicated parks funding strictly to maintaining and renovating existing parks and trails (no new facilities or land acquisition) and study up to 1 cent alongside peer-city tax/fee and park policing data.
side_a_arguments: Existing parks and recreation facilities face severe deferred maintenance deficiencies that must be addressed before building new facilities or buying land.
Raising taxes without clear maintenance priorities, police protection of park assets, and analysis of cumulative water/sewer/stormwater/solid-waste burdens could hurt low-income residents.
disagreements.side_b_position: Seek new parks facilities in addition to maintenance and renovation (initially championed by Steve Schewel before conceding a 6-1 council majority against new facilities, shifting to a 0.5-cent maintenance/renovation study).
side_b_arguments: A majority of Council still supported exploring dedicated funding for parks and trails maintenance and renovation so Council could review concrete service-level options between 0 and 0.5 cents (or up to 1 cent) during budget workshops.
Underutilized small parks could also be evaluated for repurposing rather than purely selling or abandoning.
disagreements.resolution: Councilmember Steve Schewel conceded on record that his push for new parks facilities lacked support (6-1) and moved an amended guideline—approved 7-0—directing staff to present a specific plan for parks and trails maintenance and renovation at funding levels not to exceed 1 cent per $100 assessed value.

disagreements.issue: Phillips Research Park Apartments Impact Fee Appeal – Strict Code Enforcement vs. Equitable Tolling for Neighbor Litigation Delays
disagreements.summary: Council split 6-1 in upholding staff's denial of Phillips Research Park Apartments' appeal of a $108,000 impact fee increase incurred after a competitor's zoning appeals froze the project from 2008 until building permits were filed under the higher 2009 fee schedule, with Eugene Brown dissenting and Eddie Davis exploring a compromise split.
disagreements.side_a_position: Uphold the Impact Fee Appeal Committee and staff determination applying the July 1, 2009 impact fee schedule in effect when the building permit application was submitted.
side_a_arguments: City Code strictly mandates that impact fees be calculated at the time a completed building permit application is submitted (here 2010-2011), leaving Council and the Impact Fee Appeal Committee no legal authority to retroactively apply expired 2008 rates.
While the neighboring competitor's appeals caused hardship, Planning staff followed mandatory UDO stay provisions and the application also sat with the developer for extended periods.
Granting retroactive fee relief to one developer could expose the city to legal challenges and refund demands from other developers affected by fee or regulatory changes.
disagreements.side_b_position: Defer the appeal back to the City Manager rather than upholding the higher 2009 fee assessment, citing inadequate Planning Department communication and notification to the developer.
side_b_arguments: Planning staff failed to communicate effectively with the developer regarding the impact fee change and could have communicated more forcefully regarding the neighboring owner's interconnection obligations.

Because the developer relied on 2007 staff reliance letters, closed a $23 million loan in 2008, and was stalled by third-party litigation outside its control, Council should send the matter back to the Manager for further review rather than deny relief.
disagreements.resolution: Councilmember Steve Schewel's motion to uphold the staff and Impact Fee Appeal Committee determination passed 6-1, with Councilmember Eugene Brown voting No (while Councilmember Eddie Davis noted he would have favored splitting the increase in half if legally permissible but did not offer a substitute motion after Schewel's motion carried).

meetings.title: Durham City Council March 6, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: Rescheduled to Thursday afternoon at 4:30 p.m. after Monday's regular meeting was canceled and conducted briskly due to sleet outside, the Durham City Council approved the City Manager's priority deferrals of the FY 2014-2015 budget/CIP hearing and two land-use hearings to March 17, 2014. The Council unanimously adopted the 13-item Consent Agenda (including boards and commissions appointments, a performance audit, and infrastructure and sidewalk contracts) and approved General Business Item 19 without discussion. Police Chief Jose Lopez then delivered the Durham Police Department's 2013 Annual Summary Crime Report, highlighting national CALEA and forensic accreditations, a 6% drop in Part 1 violent crime (including a 23-year low in robberies), and a 6% increase in property crime driven by larcenies.

Neither the City Attorney nor the City Clerk had priority items.

meetings.title: Durham City Council February 17, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: Meeting with six members present and one excused, the Durham City Council approved the Consent Agenda (excluding pulled Items 3 and 5) and deferred Item 3 (the roadside solicitation ordinance) to Thursday's work session following public comments and sharp council debate over panhandling enforcement versus social support. Council then approved Item 5—a ground lease agreement and parking fee ordinance for a Ninth Street lot taking effect June 1, 2014 after a three-month rent-free improvement window—and unanimously passed two public hearing land-use items: revising the 1997 Durham-Morrisville annexation agreement for the 7-acre O'Brien property and approving the consolidated annexation and initial RR zoning for Farrington Road Baptist Church.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, Excused Absence, and Snowstorm Staff Recognition
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell called the meeting to order, Council Member Eddie Davis led the Pledge of Allegiance, and Council voted 6-0 during roll call to excuse one absent member. Council postponed recognizing Southern High School's state championship football team because team members were not present. Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden announced Friday's Human Relations Awards at the Hayti Heritage Center and requested a review of the city's inclement-weather employee attendance policy, while Council Member Don Moffitt praised Public Works, Police, Fire, Solid Waste, General Services, and Fleet Management staff for 24/7 work during the recent snowstorm.

agenda_items.title: Roadside Solicitation Ordinance (Referred to Thursday Work Session)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: The City Attorney noted technical edits remained on one-way street solicitation from the driver's side, and Mayor Bell asked to refer the ordinance to Thursday's work session so he could share Springfield, Missouri's rules protecting residential areas near parks and streets from intimidation. Speakers offered contrasting views: Carolyn Schul of Principle Ministry lamented a year of postponements harming people who rely on begging for sustenance, while Victoria Peterson urged action against clusters of panhandlers hurting African-American businesses along Fayetteville Street, Roxboro Road, and Alston Avenue. Council Member Steve Schewel urged moving forward after a year of consensus work, whereas Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden argued the city needed to transform lives rather than merely allow begging, and Council voted 6-0 to defer to Thursday.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Items 3 and 5)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: After briefly reading from an outdated agenda before correcting to the current docket, Mayor Bell read the Consent Agenda covering minutes, December 2013 bid report, ESRI software maintenance, MLK Jr. Parkway and Archdale Drive traffic signal and cable installation, NCDOT Section 5303 MPO grant, Civic Software DCHC MPO website redevelopment, and North Durham Water Reclamation Facility roof replacement. Item 3 (Roadside Solicitation) and Item 5 (Ninth Street Ground Lease) were pulled for discussion, and the remainder passed unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Ground Lease Agreement (CP GPI Regency) and Ninth Street Parking Lot Fee Ordinance
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Transportation Director Mark Ahrendsen presented a revised agreement for the Ninth Street parking lot in which the lease begins March 1, 2014 but both lease payments and $1 parking fees are delayed until June 1, 2014 while the developer performs up to $30,000 in milling and striping. Ahrendsen confirmed multi-space pay stations would accept coins, currency, credit cards, and cell-phone extensions, and noted staff was working with Duke on Alley 8 improvements and OEWD on a Ninth Street business grant program. agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning's Pat Young presented a requested amendment to the 1997 Durham-Morrisville annexation agreement transferring approximately seven acres (the O'Brien property, part of KCR Developers' Kitts Creek development in Wake County/Morrisville) from Durham's annexation area to Morrisville's, effective April 1, 2014, because serving it from Durham would require a costly stream-buffer crossing on Distribution Drive. Attorney Patrick Byker spoke in support on behalf of KCR Developers LLC. Council Member Steve Schewel asked how areas of Morrisville, Chapel Hill, and Raleigh inside Durham County would be affected by any future City-County merger, with staff noting those municipalities would have to be part of merger negotiations.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation: Farrington Road Baptist Church (6004 Farrington Road)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young presented a voluntary annexation, utility extension, and initial Rural Residential (RR) zoning request for roughly eight acres at 6004 Farrington Road to allow Farrington Road Baptist Church to pursue a minor special use permit for an approximately 24,000-square-foot place of worship. Applicant representative Stark noted the church was relocating south across NC 54 near Falconbridge and that engineer Phil Cook was available. votes.item_title: Item 3: Refer Roadside Solicitation Ordinance to Thursday Work Session
votes.notes: Referred Item 3 back to Thursday's work session so the City Attorney can finalize one-way street driver-side solicitation language and Mayor Bell can present Springfield, Missouri residential protection measures.
votes.discussion_detail: The City Attorney reported that staff was still drafting a work-session revision allowing solicitation from the driver's side on one-way streets and offered council the choice of referring Item 3 to Thursday's work session or passing it with a pending amendment, noting any ordinance would not take effect for 30 days. Two speakers addressed the council: Carolyn Schul of Principle Ministry criticized a year of repeated delays hurting people who depend on panhandling for survival, while resident Victoria Peterson urged the city to address large clusters of panhandlers along Fayetteville Street, Roxboro Road, and Alston Avenue that deter customers from Black-owned businesses. Council Member Steve Schewel urged timely passage after extensive collaboration with police, attorneys, and HSAC, whereas Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden contended the city should focus on transforming lives and ending panhandling rather than enabling it. votes.notes: Lease begins March 1, 2014 with three-month payment deferral until June 1, 2014; includes $1 parking rate via numbered-space pay stations.

votes.discussion_detail: Planning staff member Pat Young presented a requested amendment to the 1997 interlocal annexation agreement with the Town of Morrisville to move roughly seven acres—the O'Brien property, part of the larger Kitts Creek project in Morrisville and Wake County—into Morrisville's annexation area effective April 1, 2014. Responding to a question from Council Member Steve Schewel about how Morrisville, Chapel Hill, and Raleigh parcels inside Durham County would be treated in any future city-county merger, Young stated those towns would need to participate in merger negotiations; the public hearing closed and Council approved the revision 6-0.

votes.item_title: Item 14: Consolidated Annexation and Initial RR Zoning — Farrington Road Baptist Church
votes.notes: Voluntary annexation, utility extension, and initial Rural Residential (RR) zoning for ~8 acres at 6004 Farrington Road for a proposed ~24,000 sq ft church.

disagreements.issue: Delaying vs. Enacting Revisions to the Roadside Solicitation (Panhandling) Ordinance (Item 3)
disagreements.summary: Public speakers and council members differed over whether to refer the revised roadside solicitation ordinance back to work session for additional residential-protection rules or enact it after a year of deliberation, as well as over the city's broader approach to panhandling.
disagreements.side_a_position: Move forward promptly with the consensus ordinance revision and allow regulated solicitation so impoverished residents are not further harmed by delays.
side_a_arguments: Stakeholders, police, the city attorney's office, and the Homeless Services Advisory Committee subcommittee spent over a year developing an alternative and reaching consensus.
Repeated postponements prolong hardship for individuals who rely on begging for sustenance (Carolyn Schul).
disagreements.side_b_position: Refer the ordinance back to work session to add residential protections and address ongoing neighborhood and business impacts rather than continuing to permit street begging.
side_b_arguments: Technical adjustments for driver-side solicitation on one-way streets were still unfinished, and Springfield, Missouri's rules protecting residents living near parks and intersections needed review (Bill Bell).
Large clusters of panhandlers along Fayetteville Street, Roxboro Road, and Alston Avenue hurt African-American business districts (Victoria Peterson).

Ellis.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Item (Refer Item 5) and Consent Agenda Approval

agenda_items.title: Confirmation of Assessment Roll for Street Paving — Clover Hill Place (Dunwoody Subdivision)

agenda_items.title: Ellis Road Residential Comprehensive Plan Amendment (A1300008) and Zoning Map Change (Z1300026)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning's Pat Young presented companion requests from T. Hankins Development to redesignate 15.53 acres at 1443 Ellis Road from Low Density Residential to Low-Medium Density Residential and rezone it from RS-20 to PDR 7.341 for 90 townhomes, including a bicycle-lane dedication and cross-access. agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change — Croasdaile Commons (Z1300024)

agenda_items.title: UDO Text Amendment — Density Revisions to Article 6 (TC1200012)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning's Michael Stock presented a privately initiated text amendment by Horvath Associates adjusting fractional density limits (up by at most 0.5 units/acre in OI/GC districts), extending the 1-unit/acre major roadway bonus to service roads with direct access and non-residential districts in suburban/compact tiers, and permitting higher RSM/RUM densities only via council-approved development plans. votes.item_title: Item 14: Zoning Map Change — Croasdaile Commons (Z1300024)
votes.notes: Rezones 8.8 acres at Croasdaile Commons on Hillandale Road from CC to CG(D) to permit ~11,000 additional sq ft of office use.
votes.discussion_detail: Pat Young presented Case Z1300024 to rezone 8.8 acres at Croasdaile Commons on Hillandale Road from Commercial Center (CC) to Commercial General with a development plan (CG(D)) to allow approximately 11,000 additional square feet of office space, noting unanimous 12-0 Planning Commission support. votes.item_title: Item 15: UDO Text Amendment — Density Revisions to Article 6 (TC1200012)
votes.notes: Privately initiated UDO text amendment by Horvath Associates rounding fractional densities and extending corridor density bonuses.
votes.discussion_detail: Michael Stock presented TC1200012, a revised Horvath Associates text amendment rounding fractional densities (e.g., from 10.5 to 11 units/acre in GC/OI), extending major roadway bonuses to service roads with access and non-residential districts in suburban compact tiers, and allowing higher RSM/RUM densities only with council-approved development plans. Proponents Ron Horvath, Jared Edens, and George Stancil argued the modest increases encourage mixed-use infill along thoroughfares like US 15-501 and Roxboro Road, while Pat Carstensen of the Inter-Neighborhood Council opposed the residential provisions as untethered to transit and walkability. Council Member Don Moffitt questioned whether raising base densities would further undercut affordable housing density bonuses, prompting Planning Director Steve Medlin to acknowledge current UDO density bonuses alone were unworkable and commit to pursuing broader cost-reducing incentives. After staff clarified to Council Member Eddie Davis that delaying the residential piece lacked clear policy direction and after Moffitt thanked Horvath and citizen reviewers for refining the text, Moffitt moved approval and Council voted 7-0.

votes.item_title: Item 16: UDO Text Amendment — Tree Coverage Calculations (TC1300002) — Continue Public Hearing to May 19, 2014
votes.notes: Reopened and continued the public hearing to May 19, 2014 so staff and applicant Horvath Associates can model acreage thresholds and affected parcels.
votes.discussion_detail: Michael Stock presented TC1300002, a Horvath Associates proposal excluding utility easements 50 feet or wider from gross tract area when calculating suburban residential tree coverage, which Horvath, Jared Edens, and George Stancil argued unfairly penalized projects like the 400-acre Del Webb Carolina Arbors site crossed by a 350-foot power easement. Environmental advocates Will Wilson, Bob Healy, Pat Carstensen, and John Tarantino (paraphrasing Joni Mitchell) strongly opposed the amendment, warning it reduces urban canopy and respiratory health benefits, lets developers count easements for density and imperviousness while shedding tree requirements, and lacks parcel mapping along New Hope Creek, Ellerbe Creek, and the Eno River. Council Member Steve Schewel stated he could not support a universal exemption for large tracts, while Council Member Don Moffitt floated limiting relief by tract acreage or easement percentage and Council Member Diane Catotti asked staff whether targeted thresholds were feasible within 90 days. After Mayor Bell emphasized that requesting additional modeling did not commit council to eventual approval, Council voted 7-0 to reopen and continue the public hearing to May 19, 2014.

disagreements.issue: Article 6 UDO Density Revisions and Impact on Transit-Oriented Growth & Affordable Housing (TC1200012)
disagreements.summary: During the public hearing on Item 15, the Inter-Neighborhood Council opposed residential density increases unrelated to transit access, and Council Members Don Moffitt and Eddie Davis scrutinized whether raising baseline densities undermined affordable housing bonuses or warranted delaying residential provisions.
disagreements.side_a_position: Adopt the revised Article 6 density adjustments and corridor bonuses as proposed by Horvath Associates and Planning staff.
side_a_arguments: Rounding fractional densities (at most 0.5 units/acre) and extending roadway bonuses to service roads and commercial/office districts encourages mixed-use redevelopment along major corridors.
Any higher density in RSM/RUM districts still requires a development plan approved by City Council, and service-road bonuses require direct access.
Density bonuses in the UDO can stack cumulatively, and affordable housing requires broader tools beyond density alone (Steve Medlin).
disagreements.side_b_position: Delay or reject the residential density provisions until density is directed toward walkable, transit-served areas and affordable housing bonuses are protected.
side_b_arguments: Allowing extra residential density outside transit corridors risks car-dependent sprawl (Pat Carstensen / Inter-Neighborhood Council).
Increasing by-right or baseline unit counts could reduce developers' incentive to use the affordable housing density bonus (questioned by Don Moffitt).
disagreements.resolution: Following staff clarifications that development plans still come before Council and that Planning will pursue non-density affordable housing incentives, Council unanimously approved TC1200012 by a 7-0 vote.

disagreements.issue: Excluding Wide Utility Easements from Tree Coverage Calculations (TC1300002)
disagreements.summary: Council and public speakers divided sharply over Horvath Associates' proposal to exclude utility easements of 50 feet or wider from tree-coverage calculations while still counting those easements toward residential density and impervious-surface allowances.
disagreements.side_a_position: Exclude wide utility easements (minus the first 50 feet) from gross tract area when calculating required tree coverage.
side_a_arguments: Power companies prohibit tree planting in wide transmission easements, forcing developers to set aside extra buildable acreage (e.g., 7.5 acres at Del Webb Carolina Arbors) to meet tree-coverage minimums.
Existing UDO exemptions already exclude ponds and road-widening rights-of-way where trees cannot be planted.
Preserving usable acreage lowers site development costs and improves housing affordability (Ron Horvath, Jared Edens, George Stancil).
disagreements.side_b_position: Reject or restrict the universal easement exemption so tree canopy is not reduced on large developments or near sensitive watersheds without parcel-level analysis.
side_b_arguments: Developers continue to receive full density and impervious-surface credit from the easement while shedding the corresponding tree-coverage obligation, harming air quality and raising urban temperatures (Will Wilson, Steve Schewel).
Staff had not mapped affected parcels near protected watersheds such as New Hope Creek, Ellerbe Creek, and the Eno River (Bob Healy, Pat Carstensen).
While small tracts encumbered by wide power easements might merit relief, there is no clear public interest in reducing tree requirements for very large developments (Steve Schewel).
disagreements.resolution: Unable to support the text amendment as drafted, Council voted 7-0 to reopen and continue the public hearing to May 19, 2014 so staff and the applicant could map affected parcels and model tract-size or percentage thresholds.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting January 21, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: With Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden presiding in Mayor Bill Bell's excused absence and snow/sleet outside, the Durham City Council expedited a 6-0 unanimous slate of major economic, land-use, and parking actions. Council approved a $600,000 capital-investment incentive contract with biopharmaceutical firm Argos Therapeutics (projected to add 178 jobs and $1.69 million in net tax revenue over 10 years), passed the Montclair Phase II annexation and 24-home rezoning over a neighbor's request for a 1,000-foot chain-link fence, and approved the Meadows at Southpoint II plan amendment and 185-unit rezoning with a vinyl-siding ban and $500 school proffer. On pulled Consent Item 5, following downtown residents' protests over ending free parking and legal advice against retroactive 2008 cutoffs, Council compromised 6-0 on a five-year half-price phase-in for all current downtown residents through December 31, 2018.

agenda_items.title: Call to Order, Roll Call, Mayor's Excused Absence, and Civil Rights Recognitions
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden called the meeting to order at 7:02 p.m., announced the Joseph Becton memorial resolution was held due to snow and sleet, and Council voted 6-0 to grant Mayor Bill Bell an excused absence to attend the U.S. Conference of Mayors meeting. Council Member Don Moffitt commended DPD's restraint during Sunday protests and noted the MLK march, while Council Member Eddie Davis recognized Royal Ice Cream sit-in participant Virginia Williams and documentarian Dr. Steve Channing following a New York Times obituary of Franklin McCain.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Item 5)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Pro Tempore Cole-McFadden read Consent Agenda Items 1 through 4 covering City Council minutes, 2013 municipal primary and election items with the Durham County Board of Elections, and two Workforce Investment Act contracts with Educational Data Systems, Inc. Item 5 (Ordinance to Change Parking Fees) was pulled to be heard after the public hearings, and Items 1 through 4 passed unanimously.

agenda_items.title: Economic Development Incentive Contract — Argos Therapeutics, Inc.
agenda_items.discussion_summary: OEWD's Kevin Dick presented a $600,000, seven-year performance-based capital investment incentive for biopharmaceutical firm Argos Therapeutics on Alexander Drive, noting projected net tax revenue of $1.69 million over 10 years, an increased commitment from 118 to 178 net new jobs over three years, and workforce/local-business recruitment plans. Chamber of Commerce representative Ted Connor and NCCU BRITE Center's Dr. Li-An Yeh joined Argos officials in support, highlighting personalized kidney cancer immunotherapies and local hiring. Council praised Durham County's matching role and the project's job quality, passing the contract 6-0 by voice vote after the electronic system failed to register.

agenda_items.title: Montclair Phase II — Utility Extension, Voluntary Annexation, and Initial Zoning (14.89 Acres)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young presented three companion actions for Montclair Phase II (Barbee Chapel and Farrington Mill Roads) to annex and zone 14.89 acres PDR 2.00/RR for up to 24 single-family homes, correcting the annexation ordinance effective date to March 31, 2014. Applicant Jared Edens (for David Weekley Homes) proffered $1,500 to Durham Public Schools prior to final plat and a 25-foot undisturbed buffer along the property line with neighbor Michael Hining, who opposed the project without a 1,000-foot chain-link fence to keep children away from his farm ponds and fruit trees. After Council Member Steve Schewel noted the difficulty of deciding on the fence, Council passed all three actions 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Comprehensive Plan Amendment — Meadows at Southpoint II (A1300007)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young presented Case A1300007 by Meadows Land Investment LLC to amend the Future Land Use Map for 46.9 acres at NC 54 and Barbee Road from Office and Commercial to Low-Medium Density Residential, which Planning Commission recommended 13-1. Hunter's Wood neighborhood representative George Bryan and applicant attorney Ken Spaulding spoke in support of the residential designation, and Council approved the amendment 6-0.

agenda_items.title: Zoning Map Change — Meadows at Southpoint II (Z1300020)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pat Young presented Case Z1300020 rezoning 46.9 acres at NC 54 and Barbee Road from RR and OI to PDR 4.718 for up to 185 residential units with stormwater aeration, a 100-foot perimeter buffer, bike-lane asphalt, a bus pull-out/shelter, and road improvements. George Bryan supported the owner-occupied townhome shift but requested changing the full-access Barbee Road driveway to right-in/right-out or adding warning signs; Transportation's Bill Judge explained sight-distance constraints were to the left so right-in/right-out would not resolve them and NCDOT would enforce sight-distance and signage at site plan. At Council Member Diane Catotti's prompting (reflecting Mayor Bell's prior request), applicant Jim Anderson and George Stancil agreed to prohibit vinyl siding in favor of cementitious siding, and Council Member Steve Schewel secured a $500 school proffer prior to approval.

agenda_items.title: Ordinance to Change Downtown Parking Fees (5-Year Half-Price Phase-In for Current Residents)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Pulled from the Consent Agenda by downtown residents William 'Coke' Ariail and Kate Dobbs, who argued ending free parking broke a city promise and imposed financial hardship on early downtown homeowners. City Attorney Patrick Baker advised that distinguishing pre-2008 'pioneer' residents from post-2008 residents would be legally arbitrary and capricious, whereas treating all current residents alike as a phase-out group distinct from future residents was defensible under local legislation. Transportation's Mark Ahrendsen also noted the Corcoran Street deck and surface lot operated as one facility, though Council Member Don Moffitt urged surface-lot pricing and a 10-year phase-in; Council compromised on Moffitt's motion (seconded by Steve Schewel) extending Option 2's 50% discount from three years to five years through December 31, 2018.

Council Member Steve Schewel also secured a $500 school-mitigation proffer at site plan approval before Council voted 6-0 to approve the rezoning.

disagreements.issue: Montclair Phase II Boundary: 1,000-Foot Chain-Link Fence vs. 25-Foot Undisturbed Buffer (Item 7)
disagreements.summary: Adjacent property owner Michael Hining urged Council to reject Montclair Phase II unless the developer built a 1,000-foot chain-link fence separating the subdivision from his 12-acre farm, whereas the developer refused the fence and offered a 25-foot undisturbed buffer.
disagreements.side_a_position: Approve the rezoning with a 25-foot undisturbed buffer along the shared property line without requiring a chain-link fence.
side_a_arguments: A chain-link fence is ineffective because people can climb over or walk around it, and law enforcement already addresses trespassing.
Requiring fences along every property line with potential foot traffic would set an unworkable precedent across Durham.
A 25-foot undisturbed buffer adds 15 feet beyond the 10-foot code minimum and benefits both the neighbor and new homeowners (Jared Edens for David Weekley Homes).
disagreements.side_b_position: Deny the rezoning unless the developer installs a chain-link fence along the 1,000-foot boundary.
side_b_arguments: The neighboring 12-acre farm contains ponds and over 50 fruit trees that pose an attractive nuisance and child safety hazard.
Phase II doubles the nearby housing count and number of children, and a 25-foot buffer or no-trespassing signs will not stop children from entering the farm (Michael Hining).
disagreements.resolution: While Council Member Steve Schewel acknowledged struggling with the request, Council accepted the 25-foot undisturbed buffer proffer and approved Montclair Phase II 6-0.

disagreements.issue: Length and Scope of Downtown Resident Parking Fee Phase-Out (Item 5)
disagreements.summary: Downtown residents, council members, and the City Attorney debated whether early downtown residents could retain free or discounted parking, how long a half-rate phase-in should last, and whether post-2008 residents could be excluded.
disagreements.side_a_position: Provide an extended multi-year half-price phase-in for current downtown residents (Don Moffitt initially favored 10 years, plus surface-lot rate relief; Coke Ariail/Kate Dobbs sought preservation of free parking).
side_a_arguments: Early downtown homeowners bought properties relying on city promises of free parking and helped revitalize downtown and grow property tax receipts (William 'Coke' Ariail, Kate Dobbs).

Charging full rates immediately asks ~130 downtown residents—who already pay higher downtown tax rates—for an extra $100,000/year, and Main Street residents prefer surface parking for safety (Don Moffitt).
disagreements.side_b_position: Limit subsidies to pre-2008 'pioneer' residents if legally possible, or keep the phase-out brief to avoid larger revenue losses.
side_b_arguments: Residents moving in after 2008 were aware of changing policies and should not receive the same long-term subsidy as the ~21 original pioneers (Steve Schewel).
Extending the 50% discount beyond three years costs the city approximately $50,000 in foregone revenue per additional year (clarified by Diane Catotti).
Legally, a retroactive 2008 cutoff would be arbitrary and capricious, leaving a uniform phase-out for all current residents as the only defensible option (City Attorney).
disagreements.resolution: Council compromised 6-0 on Don Moffitt's motion, seconded by Steve Schewel, adopting Option 2 with a five-year half-price phase-in for all current downtown residents through December 31, 2018.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting January 6, 2014
meetings.executive_summary: At its first meeting of 2014, following a 5:30 p.m. closed session, Mayor Bill Bell announced that the Durham City Council voted unanimously pursuant to NCGS 160A-168(c)(7) to concur with City Manager Tom Bonfield's decision to release a summary report of the Durham Police Department's Internal Affairs investigation into the November 19, 2013 death of Jesus Huerta, while awaiting the pending SBI and medical examiner reports. Council deferred the Meadows at Southpoint II hearings to January 21 due to a newspaper notice error (with Mayor Bell flagging opposition to vinyl siding), adopted the Consent Agenda excluding pulled Items 8 and 9, and approved both pulled items (the SystemVision energy agreement and transferring two city lots to Habitat for Humanity) 7-0. During the FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan public hearing (received 7-0), speakers pressed for youth job training, permanent supportive housing, and Northeast Central Durham investment, and CAARE Inc.'s Sharon Elliott-Bynum challenged Continuum of Care scoring procedures—prompting Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden to demand a full investigation at Thursday's work session.

agenda_items.title: Committee Appointments and Unanimous Closed-Session Action to Release Jesus Huerta Internal Affairs Report

Mayor Bell then reported that in a 5:30 p.m. closed session, Council voted unanimously under NCGS 160A-168(c)(7) to concur with City Manager Tom Bonfield's recommendation to release a written summary of DPD's Internal Affairs investigation into the November 19, 2013 death of Jesus Huerta later that week (first sharing it with the family's attorney), while noting the separate SBI investigation remained pending the medical examiner's report.

agenda_items.title: City Manager Priority Items: Defer Items 16 and 17 (Meadows at Southpoint II) to January 21, 2014
agenda_items.discussion_summary: City Manager Tom Bonfield requested deferring Item 16 (Comprehensive Plan Amendment, Meadows at Southpoint 2) and Item 17 (Zoning Map Change, Meadows at Southpoint 2) to January 21, 2014 due to a newspaper advertisement notification error, which Council approved 7-0. Mayor Bell noted he would miss the January 21 meeting for the U.S. Conference of Mayors and asked colleagues to examine the project's construction materials and prohibit vinyl siding.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Excluding Pulled Items 8 and 9)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bell read Consent Agenda Items 1 through 14 covering council minutes, Appearance Commission and Durham Housing Authority appointments, the memorial resolution for Joseph Becton, Jr., November 2013 bid report, street acceptances, Clover Hill Place paving preliminary assessment roll, SystemVision agreement (Item 8, questioned by Mayor Bell), Habitat for Humanity lot transfer (Item 9, pulled), pumper truck and loader truck purchases, asphaltic concrete extension, Upper Neuse River Basin Association nutrient credit project, and household hazardous waste contract amendment #5. agenda_items.title: FY 2014-2015 Annual Action Plan Needs Public Hearing (CDBG, HOME, and ESG)

agenda_items.title: SystemVision Program Agreement (NCHFA, City of Durham, and Advanced Energy Corporation)

agenda_items.title: Ownership Transfer of Two City-Owned Lots in Southwest Central Durham to Habitat for Humanity of Durham, Inc.

votes.item_title: Item 8 (Pulled): SystemVision Program Agreement (NCHFA, City of Durham, and Advanced Energy Corporation)

votes.discussion_detail: Council turned to pulled Consent Item 9 transferring ownership of two city-owned lots in Southwest Central Durham to Habitat for Humanity of Durham, Inc. disagreements.issue: Continuum of Care / Homeless Funding Scoring Fairness and Transparency (Item 15)
disagreements.summary: During the Annual Action Plan public hearing, nonprofit leader Sharon Elliott-Bynum challenged the fairness and transparency of Community Development's Continuum of Care funding recommendations, prompting Council scrutiny despite staff explaining it was a separate process from CDBG/HOME/ESG.
disagreements.side_a_position: Investigate and reform funding recommendations to ensure fair scoring, process clarity, and inclusion of smaller/new nonprofits such as female veterans housing.
side_a_arguments: CAARE Inc.'s proposal to rehab a home for four homeless female veterans scored an average of 85 from the Citizens Advisory Committee compared to 84 for the staff-recommended agency, yet was passed over (Sharon Elliott-Bynum).
The recommended project was part two of a renewal rather than a new project, and an earlier $28,000 award from 2008-09 was never disbursed after the prior director's death (Sharon Elliott-Bynum).

Council must fully investigate the process at Thursday's work session because having the same organizations receive funding repeatedly does not appear fair (Cora Cole-McFadden; follow-up also requested by Bill Bell).
disagreements.side_b_position: Clarify that Continuum of Care recommendations follow a separate HUD process overseen by the Homeless Services Advisory Committee rather than the CDBG/HOME/ESG Annual Action Plan.
side_b_arguments: The funding cited by Ms. Bynum comes from the Continuum of Care process scheduled before the Homeless Services Advisory Committee, which makes recommendations separately from the Annual Action Plan hearing (Community Development Director Reginald Johnson).
Staff would research the historical $28,000 award question separately.
disagreements.resolution: Council voted 7-0 to receive all public hearing comments while directing Community Development staff to investigate Ms. Bynum's complaints and report back at Thursday's work session.

meetings.title: Durham City Council Meeting December 16, 2013
meetings.executive_summary: The Durham City Council opened its final meeting of 2013 by honoring Nelson Mandela, recognizing the Absolute Care Foundation for renovating Carroll Street Park, and commemorating the 50th anniversary of a 1963 Durham civil rights advertisement. Council then heard the third-quarter crime report amid pointed public and council discussion regarding police transparency, traffic-stop racial disparities, and pending State Bureau of Investigation inquiries into critical incidents. In land-use business, Council approved 11 annexation, comprehensive plan, zoning, and street-closing items, including two residential projects with voluntary per-student contributions to Durham Public Schools and a contentious 5-2 approval (reconsidered and re-approved 5-2 with a brick-exterior commitment) for a Murphy USA gas station in Hope Valley Farms. Council also approved three pulled consent items, with Mayor Pro Tempore Cora Cole-McFadden dissenting 6-1 on awarding a Workforce Investment Act youth contract to a non-Durham firm.

agenda_items.title: Nelson Mandela Proclamation, Absolute Care Foundation Recognition, and 1963 Civil Rights Commemoration
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell presented a proclamation honoring the life and legacy of Nelson Mandela alongside resident Owen Scott and a tribute video by Nina Leonard. Parks and Recreation Director Rhonda Parker and Conrad Rensburg of the Absolute Care Foundation were recognized for their $14,680 donation and multi-year adoption of Carroll Street Park. Council Member Eddie Davis also recognized the 50th anniversary of the 1963 full-page newspaper advertisement urging Durham merchants to integrate public facilities.

agenda_items.title: Consent Agenda (Items 1, 3, 5-9, 13)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Mayor Bill Bell read the consent agenda headings, including minutes, a WIA youth contract, Durham Arts Council building and services agreement, Carroll Street Park donation acceptance, D3 Community Outreach lease, Holton School interlocal amendment with Durham Public Schools, Holland Alley easement, and sewer-use ordinance revisions. Council pulled Items 4, 10, and 11 for separate consideration before adopting the remaining consent items.

agenda_items.title: 2013 Third Quarter Crime Summary Report
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Police Chief Jose Lopez reported that Part 1 index crimes were at a 14-year low for the first nine months of 2013, with violent crime down 8%, burglaries down 6%, and the department achieving CALEA Gold Standard Accreditation. Resident Victoria Peterson criticized police leadership over recent homicides and lawsuits, while Council Members Steve Schewel, Eddie Davis, Don Moffitt, and Mayor Bill Bell praised officers' community care work while pressing for greater transparency, non-defensive engagement with FADE's traffic-stop data, and faster public release of facts in the Jesus Huerta, Derek Walker, and Jose Ocampo cases.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation Item: Oaks at Lyons Farm
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a utility extension agreement, voluntary contiguous annexation, and initial Rural Residential zoning for 17 single-family homes on 9.4 acres off Scott King Road. Lyons Farm resident Jeff Dozier opposed the layout because all traffic would route through Silk Tree Lane and Silver Pine Court rather than adding a Scott King Road entrance, while applicant Jarrod Edens cited NCDOT access constraints and 50% open space preservation and proffered $1,500 per additional student to Durham Public Schools.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation Item: Richmond Park
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented a utility extension agreement, voluntary annexation, and initial RS-10(D) zoning for 15 single-family detached lots previously approved by Durham County in 2009. Adjacent homeowners Matthew Willis, Charles Cheney, and Bill Hunt raised concerns about multi-day stormwater runoff, detention pond mosquitoes, and tree clearing along the northern boundary; attorney Michael Birch noted the site detains up to the 100-year storm and proffered an undisturbed 10-foot tree coverage buffer along the northern line.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation Item: RTP Global Mission Church (BDG-130016)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented a utility extension agreement, voluntary contiguous annexation, and initial Industrial Light zoning to allow a place of worship by right for RTP Global Mission Church. Church representative Stephen Park attended to answer questions, and Council Member Don Moffitt confirmed the presence of steep slopes toward an adjacent stream before the hearing closed without opposition.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation Item: Grovery NC
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented a utility extension agreement, voluntary non-contiguous annexation, and initial RS-20 zoning for a single-family residential lot. Representative Cliff Cradle explained that the lot lacked space for private well and septic and lay directly on the city border; no public opposition was raised.

agenda_items.title: Consolidated Annexation Item: Changing Hearts for Changing Lives (BDG-130017)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented a utility extension agreement, voluntary contiguous annexation (effective December 31, 2013), and initial Rural Residential zoning for a proposed church requiring a minor special use permit from the Board of Adjustment. Neighbor David Johnson questioned sewer extension costs, site plans, and stream flooding; staff clarified that the applicant funds utility extensions and that regulated 50- to 100-foot stream buffers and Board of Adjustment notice apply.

agenda_items.title: Comprehensive Plan Amendment: Page Park 2 (A13-0006)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented Lennar Carolinas' request to amend the Future Land Use Map for an approximately 10-acre parcel from Office to Medium Density Residential as a transition between industrial/commercial uses and lower-density residential areas. agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented Lennar Carolinas' companion rezoning of 16.87 acres on Jessup Street to Residential Suburban Multifamily with a Development Plan for up to 124 units. Following questions from Council Members Steve Schewel and Don Moffitt regarding school impacts and impervious surface rules in the Crabtree Creek Basin, the applicant proffered a $500 contribution per additional student to Durham Public Schools calculated at site plan.

agenda_items.title: Comprehensive Plan Amendment: Muirfield Commercial (A12-0015)
agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented Horvath Associates' request to amend 1.85 acres on Guess Road from Low/Medium Density Residential to Commercial. agenda_items.discussion_summary: Staff presented a Commercial Neighborhood development plan modification for 2.95 acres at 1439 Victory Boulevard increasing permitted non-residential floor area from 5,000 to 8,000 square feet and allowing mixed office, retail, and non-drive-through restaurant uses. agenda_items.discussion_summary: Planning staff presented Davis Moore Capital's request to rezone 7.99 acres at 117 East NC 54 Highway from RS-20 to Office and Institutional with a Development Plan for up to 150,000 square feet of office space, including a 4-foot bicycle lane commitment. Transportation staff answered Council Member Steve Schewel's traffic questions, noting NC 54 remained below Level of Service D capacity with no direct site access to I-40 or Fayetteville Road.
